./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:440:///
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:441:/// The builder supports a large number of configurable options. This includes
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:442:/// specific glob overrides, file type matching, toggling whether hidden
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:443:/// files are ignored or not, and of course, support for respecting gitignore
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:444:/// files.
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:445:///
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:446:/// By default, all ignore files found are respected. This includes `.ignore`,
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:447:/// `.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude` and even your global gitignore
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:448:/// globs, usually found in `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore`.
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:449:///
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:450:/// Some standard recursive directory options are also supported, such as
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:451:/// limiting the recursive depth or whether to follow symbolic links (disabled
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:452:/// by default).
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:453:///
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:454:/// # Ignore rules
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:455:///
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:456:/// There are many rules that influence whether a particular file or directory
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:457:/// is skipped by this iterator. Those rules are documented here. Note that
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:458:/// the rules assume a default configuration.
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:459:///
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:460:/// * First, glob overrides are checked. If a path matches a glob override,
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:461:/// then matching stops. The path is then only skipped if the glob that matched
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:462:/// the path is an ignore glob. (An override glob is a whitelist glob unless it
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:463:/// starts with a `!`, in which case it is an ignore glob.)
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:464:/// * Second, ignore files are checked. Ignore files currently only come from
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:465:/// git ignore files (`.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude` and the configured
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:466:/// global gitignore file), plain `.ignore` files, which have the same format
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:467:/// as gitignore files, or explicitly added ignore files. The precedence order
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:468:/// is: `.ignore`, `.gitignore`, `.git/info/exclude`, global gitignore and
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:469:/// finally explicitly added ignore files. Note that precedence between
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:470:/// different types of ignore files is not impacted by the directory hierarchy;
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:471:/// any `.ignore` file overrides all `.gitignore` files. Within each precedence
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:472:/// level, more nested ignore files have a higher precedence than less nested
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:473:/// ignore files.
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:474:/// * Third, if the previous step yields an ignore match, then all matching
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:475:/// is stopped and the path is skipped. If it yields a whitelist match, then
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:476:/// matching continues. A whitelist match can be overridden by a later matcher.
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:477:/// * Fourth, unless the path is a directory, the file type matcher is run on
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:478:/// the path. As above, if it yields an ignore match, then all matching is
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:479:/// stopped and the path is skipped. If it yields a whitelist match, then
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:480:/// matching continues.
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:481:/// * Fifth, if the path hasn't been whitelisted and it is hidden, then the
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:482:/// path is skipped.
./crates/ignore/src/walk.rs:483:/// * Sixth, unless the path is a directory, the size of the file is compared

async def _send_handling_auth(
        self,
        request: Request,
        auth: Auth,
        follow_redirects: bool,
        history: list[Response],
    ) -> Response:
        auth_flow = auth.async_auth_flow(request)
        try:
            request = await auth_flow.__anext__()

            while True:
                response = await self._send_handling_redirects(
                    request,
                    follow_redirects=follow_redirects,
                    history=history,
                )
                try:
                    try:
                        next_request = await auth_flow.asend(response)
                    except StopAsyncIteration:
                        return response

                    response.history = list(history)
                    await response.aread()
                    request = next_request
                    history.append(response)

                except BaseException as exc:
                    await response.aclose()
                    raise exc
        finally:
            await auth_flow.aclose()

    async def send(
        self,
        request: Request,
        *,
        stream: bool = False,
        auth: AuthTypes | UseClientDefault | None = USE_CLIENT_DEFAULT,
        follow_redirects: bool | UseClientDefault = USE_CLIENT_DEFAULT,
    ) -> Response:
        """
        Send a request.

        The request is sent as-is, unmodified.

        Typically you'll want to build one with `AsyncClient.build_request()`
        so that any client-level configuration is merged into the request,
        but passing an explicit `httpx.Request()` is supported as well.

        See also: [Request instances][0]

        [0]: /advanced/clients/#request-instances
        """
        if self._state == ClientState.CLOSED:
            raise RuntimeError("Cannot send a request, as the client has been closed.")

        self._state = ClientState.OPENED
        follow_redirects = (
            self.follow_redirects
            if isinstance(follow_redirects, UseClientDefault)
            else follow_redirects
        )

        self._set_timeout(request)

        auth = self._build_request_auth(request, auth)

        response = await self._send_handling_auth(
            request,
            auth=auth,
            follow_redirects=follow_redirects,
            history=[],
        )
        try:
            if not stream:
                await response.aread()

            return response

        except BaseException as exc:
            await response.aclose()
            raise exc

    async def _send_handling_auth(
        self,
        request: Request,
        auth: Auth,
        follow_redirects: bool,
        history: list[Response],
    ) -> Response:
        auth_flow = auth.async_auth_flow(request)
        try:
            request = await auth_flow.__anext__()

            while True:
                response = await self._send_handling_redirects(
                    request,
                    follow_redirects=follow_redirects,
                    history=history,
                )
                try:
                    try:
                        next_request = await auth_flow.asend(response)
                    except StopAsyncIteration:
                        return response

                    response.history = list(history)
                    await response.aread()
                    request = next_request
                    history.append(response)

                except BaseException as exc:
                    await response.aclose()
                    raise exc
        finally:
            await auth_flow.aclose()

    async def _send_handling_redirects(
        self,
        request: Request,
        follow_redirects: bool,
        history: list[Response],
    ) -> Response:
        while True:
            if len(history) > self.max_redirects:
                raise TooManyRedirects(
                    "Exceeded maximum allowed redirects.", request=request
                )

class Auth:
    """
    Base class for all authentication schemes.

    To implement a custom authentication scheme, subclass `Auth` and override
    the `.auth_flow()` method.

    If the authentication scheme does I/O such as disk access or network calls, or uses
    synchronization primitives such as locks, you should override `.sync_auth_flow()`
    and/or `.async_auth_flow()` instead of `.auth_flow()` to provide specialized
    implementations that will be used by `Client` and `AsyncClient` respectively.
    """

    requires_request_body = False
    requires_response_body = False

    def auth_flow(self, request: Request) -> typing.Generator[Request, Response, None]:
        """
        Execute the authentication flow.

        To dispatch a request, `yield` it:

        ```
        yield request
        ```

        The client will `.send()` the response back into the flow generator. You can
        access it like so:

        ```
        response = yield request
        ```

        A `return` (or reaching the end of the generator) will result in the
        client returning the last response obtained from the server.

        You can dispatch as many requests as is necessary.
        """
        yield request

    def sync_auth_flow(
        self, request: Request
    ) -> typing.Generator[Request, Response, None]:
        """
        Execute the authentication flow synchronously.

        By default, this defers to `.auth_flow()`. You should override this method
        when the authentication scheme does I/O and/or uses concurrency primitives.
        """
        if self.requires_request_body:
            request.read()

        flow = self.auth_flow(request)
        request = next(flow)

        while True:
            response = yield request
            if self.requires_response_body:
                response.read()

            try:
                request = flow.send(response)
            except StopIteration:
                break

    async def async_auth_flow(
        self, request: Request
    ) -> typing.AsyncGenerator[Request, Response]:
        """
        Execute the authentication flow asynchronously.

        By default, this defers to `.auth_flow()`. You should override this method
        when the authentication scheme does I/O and/or uses concurrency primitives.
        """
        if self.requires_request_body:
            await request.aread()

        flow = self.auth_flow(request)
        request = next(flow)

        while True:
            response = yield request
            if self.requires_response_body:
                await response.aread()

            try:
                request = flow.send(response)
            except StopIteration:
                break

class Auth:
    """
    Base class for all authentication schemes.

    To implement a custom authentication scheme, subclass `Auth` and override
    the `.auth_flow()` method.

    If the authentication scheme does I/O such as disk access or network calls, or uses
    synchronization primitives such as locks, you should override `.sync_auth_flow()`
    and/or `.async_auth_flow()` instead of `.auth_flow()` to provide specialized
    implementations that will be used by `Client` and `AsyncClient` respectively.
    """

    requires_request_body = False
    requires_response_body = False

    def auth_flow(self, request: Request) -> typing.Generator[Request, Response, None]:
        """
        Execute the authentication flow.

        To dispatch a request, `yield` it:

        ```
        yield request
        ```

        The client will `.send()` the response back into the flow generator. You can
        access it like so:

        ```
        response = yield request
        ```

        A `return` (or reaching the end of the generator) will result in the
        client returning the last response obtained from the server.

        You can dispatch as many requests as is necessary.
        """
        yield request

    def sync_auth_flow(
        self, request: Request
    ) -> typing.Generator[Request, Response, None]:
        """
        Execute the authentication flow synchronously.

        By default, this defers to `.auth_flow()`. You should override this method
        when the authentication scheme does I/O and/or uses concurrency primitives.
        """
        if self.requires_request_body:
            request.read()

        flow = self.auth_flow(request)
        request = next(flow)

        while True:
            response = yield request
            if self.requires_response_body:
                response.read()

            try:
                request = flow.send(response)
            except StopIteration:
                break

    async def async_auth_flow(
        self, request: Request
    ) -> typing.AsyncGenerator[Request, Response]:
        """
        Execute the authentication flow asynchronously.

        By default, this defers to `.auth_flow()`. You should override this method
        when the authentication scheme does I/O and/or uses concurrency primitives.
        """
        if self.requires_request_body:
            await request.aread()

        flow = self.auth_flow(request)
        request = next(flow)

        while True:
            response = yield request
            if self.requires_response_body:
                await response.aread()

            try:
                request = flow.send(response)
            except StopIteration:
                break

        """
        Send a request.

        The request is sent as-is, unmodified.

        Typically you'll want to build one with `AsyncClient.build_request()`
        so that any client-level configuration is merged into the request,
        but passing an explicit `httpx.Request()` is supported as well.

        See also: [Request instances][0]

        [0]: /advanced/clients/#request-instances
        """
        if self._state == ClientState.CLOSED:
            raise RuntimeError("Cannot send a request, as the client has been closed.")

        self._state = ClientState.OPENED
        follow_redirects = (
            self.follow_redirects
            if isinstance(follow_redirects, UseClientDefault)
            else follow_redirects
        )

        self._set_timeout(request)

        auth = self._build_request_auth(request, auth)

        response = await self._send_handling_auth(
            request,
            auth=auth,
            follow_redirects=follow_redirects,
            history=[],
        )
        try:
            if not stream:
                await response.aread()

            return response

        except BaseException as exc:
            await response.aclose()
            raise exc

    async def _send_handling_auth(
        self,
        request: Request,
        auth: Auth,
        follow_redirects: bool,
        history: list[Response],
    ) -> Response:
        auth_flow = auth.async_auth_flow(request)
        try:
            request = await auth_flow.__anext__()

            while True:
                response = await self._send_handling_redirects(
                    request,
                    follow_redirects=follow_redirects,
                    history=history,
                )
                try:
                    try:
                        next_request = await auth_flow.asend(response)
                    except StopAsyncIteration:
                        return response

                    response.history = list(history)
                    await response.aread()
                    request = next_request
                    history.append(response)

                except BaseException as exc:
                    await response.aclose()
                    raise exc
        finally:
            await auth_flow.aclose()

    async def _send_handling_redirects(
        self,
        request: Request,
        follow_redirects: bool,
        history: list[Response],
    ) -> Response:
        while True:
            if len(history) > self.max_redirects:
                raise TooManyRedirects(

from __future__ import annotations

from enum import IntEnum

__all__ = ["codes"]


class codes(IntEnum):
    """HTTP status codes and reason phrases

    Status codes from the following RFCs are all observed:

        * RFC 7231: Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP/1.1), obsoletes 2616
        * RFC 6585: Additional HTTP Status Codes
        * RFC 3229: Delta encoding in HTTP
        * RFC 4918: HTTP Extensions for WebDAV, obsoletes 2518
        * RFC 5842: Binding Extensions to WebDAV
        * RFC 7238: Permanent Redirect
        * RFC 2295: Transparent Content Negotiation in HTTP
        * RFC 2774: An HTTP Extension Framework
        * RFC 7540: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)
        * RFC 2324: Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)
        * RFC 7725: An HTTP Status Code to Report Legal Obstacles
        * RFC 8297: An HTTP Status Code for Indicating Hints
        * RFC 8470: Using Early Data in HTTP
    """

    def __new__(cls, value: int, phrase: str = "") -> codes:
        obj = int.__new__(cls, value)
        obj._value_ = value

        obj.phrase = phrase  # type: ignore[attr-defined]
        return obj

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        return str(self.value)

    @classmethod
    def get_reason_phrase(cls, value: int) -> str:
        try:
            return codes(value).phrase  # type: ignore
        except ValueError:
            return ""

    @classmethod
    def is_informational(cls, value: int) -> bool:
        """
        Returns `True` for 1xx status codes, `False` otherwise.
        """
        return 100 <= value <= 199

    @classmethod
    def is_success(cls, value: int) -> bool:
        """
        Returns `True` for 2xx status codes, `False` otherwise.
        """
        return 200 <= value <= 299

    @classmethod
    def is_redirect(cls, value: int) -> bool:
        """
        Returns `True` for 3xx status codes, `False` otherwise.
        """
        return 300 <= value <= 399

    @classmethod
    def is_client_error(cls, value: int) -> bool:
        """
        Returns `True` for 4xx status codes, `False` otherwise.
        """
        return 400 <= value <= 499

    @classmethod
    def is_server_error(cls, value: int) -> bool:
        """
        Returns `True` for 5xx status codes, `False` otherwise.
        """
        return 500 <= value <= 599

    @classmethod

def test_multi_with_identity():
    body = b"test 123"
    compressed_body = b"\x8b\x03\x80test 123\x03"

    headers = [(b"Content-Encoding", b"br, identity")]
    response = httpx.Response(
        200,
        headers=headers,
        content=compressed_body,
    )
    assert response.content == body

    headers = [(b"Content-Encoding", b"identity, br")]
    response = httpx.Response(
        200,
        headers=headers,
        content=compressed_body,
    )
    assert response.content == body

./fuzz/README.md:1:# Fuzz Testing
./fuzz/README.md:2:
./fuzz/README.md:3:## Introduction
./fuzz/README.md:4:
./fuzz/README.md:5:Fuzz testing produces pseudo-random / arbitrary data that is used to find
./fuzz/README.md:6:stability issues within a code base. While Rust provides a strong type system,
./fuzz/README.md:7:this does not guarantee that an object will convert properly from one struct
./fuzz/README.md:8:to another. It is the responsibility of the developer to ensure that a struct
./fuzz/README.md:9:is converted properly. Fuzz testing will generate input within the domain of
./fuzz/README.md:10:each property. This arbitrary data can then be used to convert from ObjectA
./fuzz/README.md:11:to ObjectB and then back. This type of testing will help catch bugs that the
./fuzz/README.md:12:type system is not able to see.
./fuzz/README.md:13:
./fuzz/README.md:14:## Installation
./fuzz/README.md:15:
./fuzz/README.md:16:This crate relies on the `cargo-fuzz` component. To install this component,
./fuzz/README.md:17:run the following from the `fuzz` directory:
./fuzz/README.md:18:
./fuzz/README.md:19:```bash
./fuzz/README.md:20:cargo install cargo-fuzz
./fuzz/README.md:21:```
./fuzz/README.md:22:
./fuzz/README.md:23:## Listing Targets
./fuzz/README.md:24:
./fuzz/README.md:25:Once installed, fuzz targets can be listed by running the following command:
./fuzz/README.md:26:
./fuzz/README.md:27:```bash
./fuzz/README.md:28:cargo fuzz list
./fuzz/README.md:29:```
./fuzz/README.md:30:
./fuzz/README.md:31:This command will print out a list of all targets that can be tested.
./fuzz/README.md:32:
./fuzz/README.md:33:## Running Fuzz Tests
./fuzz/README.md:34:
./fuzz/README.md:35:To run a fuzz test, the target must be specified:
./fuzz/README.md:36:
./fuzz/README.md:37:```bash
./fuzz/README.md:38:cargo fuzz run <target>
./fuzz/README.md:39:```
./fuzz/README.md:40:
./fuzz/README.md:41:Note that the above will run the fuzz test indefinitely. Use the
./fuzz/README.md:42:`-max_total_time=<num seconds>` flag to specify how many seconds the test
./fuzz/README.md:43:should run for:
./fuzz/README.md:44:
./fuzz/README.md:45:```bash
./fuzz/README.md:46:cargo fuzz run <target> -- -max_total_time=5
./fuzz/README.md:47:```
./fuzz/README.md:48:
./fuzz/README.md:49:The above command will run the fuzz test for five seconds. If the test
./fuzz/README.md:50:completes without error it will show how many tests were run successfully.
./fuzz/README.md:51:The test will abort and return a non-zero error code if it is able to produce
./fuzz/README.md:52:an error. The arbitrary input will be displayed in the event of a failure.

./AI_POLICY.md:1:# AI Policy
./AI_POLICY.md:2:
./AI_POLICY.md:3:Using AI (i.e., LLMs) as tools for coding is welcome. A high bar is held for
./AI_POLICY.md:4:all contributions to this project. Moreover, the project maintainers remain
./AI_POLICY.md:5:responsible for any code that is published as part of a release. Contributors
./AI_POLICY.md:6:are expected to be responsible for any code they publish.
./AI_POLICY.md:7:
./AI_POLICY.md:8:**AI should not be used to generate comments when communicating with
./AI_POLICY.md:9:maintainers**. Comments are expected to be written by humans. Comments that are
./AI_POLICY.md:10:believed to be written by AI may be hidden without notice.
./AI_POLICY.md:11:
./AI_POLICY.md:12:If you are opening an issue, you should be able to describe the problem in your
./AI_POLICY.md:13:own words.
./AI_POLICY.md:14:
./AI_POLICY.md:15:If you are opening a pull request, you are expected to be able to explain the
./AI_POLICY.md:16:proposed changes in your own words. This includes the pull request body and
./AI_POLICY.md:17:responses to questions. **Do not copy responses from the AI when replying to
./AI_POLICY.md:18:questions from maintainers.**
./AI_POLICY.md:19:
./AI_POLICY.md:20:This project requires a human in the loop who understands the work produced by
./AI_POLICY.md:21:AI. **Autonomous agents are not allowed to be used for contributing to this
./AI_POLICY.md:22:project**. Pull requests that appear in violation of this will be closed,
./AI_POLICY.md:23:perhaps without notice.
./AI_POLICY.md:24:
./AI_POLICY.md:25:If you wish to include context from an interaction with AI in your comments, it
./AI_POLICY.md:26:must be in a quote block (e.g., using `>`) and disclosed as such. It must be
./AI_POLICY.md:27:accompanied by human commentary explaining the relevance and implications of
./AI_POLICY.md:28:the context. Do not share long snippets.
./AI_POLICY.md:29:
./AI_POLICY.md:30:AI is useful when communicating as a non-native English speaker. If you are
./AI_POLICY.md:31:using AI to edit your comments for this purpose, please take the time to ensure
./AI_POLICY.md:32:it reflects your own voice and ideas. If using AI for translation, we recommend
./AI_POLICY.md:33:writing in your native language and including the AI translation in a quote
./AI_POLICY.md:34:block.
./AI_POLICY.md:35:
./AI_POLICY.md:36:This policy was adapted from [uv's AI policy].
./AI_POLICY.md:37:
./AI_POLICY.md:38:[uv's AI policy]: https://github.com/astral-sh/.github/blob/c5187e200db51bfe11d56e13053d29bd3793fdd8/AI_POLICY.md

./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:1:# Release Checklist
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:2:
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:3:* Ensure local `master` is up to date with respect to `origin/master`.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:4:* Run `cargo update` and review dependency updates. Commit updated
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:5:  `Cargo.lock`.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:6:* Run `cargo outdated` and review semver incompatible updates. Unless there is
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:7:  a strong motivation otherwise, review and update every dependency. Also
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:8:  run `--aggressive`, but don't update to crates that are still in beta.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:9:* Update date in `crates/core/flags/doc/template.rg.1`.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:10:* Update the CHANGELOG as appropriate.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:11:* Review changes for every crate in `crates` since the last ripgrep release.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:12:  If the set of changes is non-empty, issue a new release for that crate. Check
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:13:  crates in the following order. After updating a crate, ensure minimal
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:14:  versions are updated as appropriate in dependents. If an update is required,
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:15:  run `cargo-up --no-push crates/{CRATE}/Cargo.toml`.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:16:    * crates/globset
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:17:    * crates/ignore
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:18:    * crates/cli
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:19:    * crates/matcher
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:20:    * crates/regex
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:21:    * crates/pcre2
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:22:    * crates/searcher
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:23:    * crates/printer
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:24:    * crates/grep (bump minimal versions as necessary)
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:25:    * crates/core (do **not** bump version, but update dependencies as needed)
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:26:* Edit the `Cargo.toml` to set the new ripgrep version. Run
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:27:  `cargo update -p ripgrep` so that the `Cargo.lock` is updated. Commit the
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:28:  changes and create a new signed tag. Alternatively, use
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:29:  `cargo-up --no-push --no-release Cargo.toml {VERSION}` to automate this.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:30:* Run `cargo package` and ensure it succeeds.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:31:* Push changes to GitHub, NOT including the tag. (But do not publish a new
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:32:  version of ripgrep to crates.io yet.)
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:33:* Once CI for `master` finishes successfully, push the version tag. (Trying to
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:34:  do this in one step seems to result in GitHub Actions not seeing the tag
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:35:  push and thus not running the release workflow.)
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:36:* Wait for CI to finish creating the release. If the release build fails, then
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:37:  delete the tag from GitHub, make fixes, re-tag, delete the release and push.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:38:* Copy the relevant section of the CHANGELOG to the tagged release notes.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:39:  Include this blurb describing what ripgrep is:
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:40:  > In case you haven't heard of it before, ripgrep is a line-oriented search
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:41:  > tool that recursively searches the current directory for a regex pattern.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:42:  > By default, ripgrep will respect gitignore rules and automatically skip
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:43:  > hidden files/directories and binary files.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:44:* Run `cargo publish`.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:45:* Run `ci/sha256-releases {VERSION} >> pkg/brew/ripgrep-bin.rb`. Then edit
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:46:  `pkg/brew/ripgrep-bin.rb` to update the version number and sha256 hashes.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:47:  Remove extraneous stuff added by `ci/sha256-releases`. Commit changes.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:48:* Add TBD section to the top of the CHANGELOG:
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:49:  ```
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:50:  TBD
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:51:  ===
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:52:  Unreleased changes. Release notes have not yet been written.
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:53:  ```
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:54:
./RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md:55:Note that [`cargo-up` can be found in BurntSushi's dotfiles][dotfiles].

./README.md:1:ripgrep (rg)
./README.md:2:------------
./README.md:3:ripgrep is a line-oriented search tool that recursively searches the current
./README.md:4:directory for a regex pattern. By default, ripgrep will respect gitignore rules
./README.md:5:and automatically skip hidden files/directories and binary files. (To disable
./README.md:6:all automatic filtering by default, use `rg -uuu`.) ripgrep has first class
./README.md:7:support on Windows, macOS and Linux, with binary downloads available for [every
./README.md:8:release](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases). ripgrep is similar to
./README.md:9:other popular search tools like The Silver Searcher, ack and grep.

./README.md:39:### Quick examples comparing tools
./README.md:40:
./README.md:41:This example searches the entire
./README.md:42:[Linux kernel source tree](https://github.com/BurntSushi/linux)
./README.md:43:(after running `make defconfig && make -j8`) for `[A-Z]+_SUSPEND`, where
./README.md:44:all matches must be words. Timings were collected on a system with an Intel
./README.md:45:i9-12900K 5.2 GHz.
./README.md:46:
./README.md:47:Please remember that a single benchmark is never enough! See my
./README.md:48:[blog post on ripgrep](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/)
./README.md:49:for a very detailed comparison with more benchmarks and analysis.
./README.md:50:
./README.md:51:| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
./README.md:52:| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
./README.md:53:| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | **0.082s** (1.00x) |
./README.md:54:| [hypergrep](https://github.com/p-ranav/hypergrep) | `hgrep -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.167s (2.04x) |
./README.md:55:| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `git grep -P -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.273s (3.34x) |
./README.md:56:| [The Silver Searcher](https://github.com/ggreer/the_silver_searcher) | `ag -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 534 | 0.443s (5.43x) |
./README.md:57:| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r --ignore-files --no-hidden -I -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.639s (7.82x) |
./README.md:58:| [git grep](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=C git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 0.727s (8.91x) |
./README.md:59:| [git grep (Unicode)](https://www.kernel.org/pub/software/scm/git/docs/git-grep.html) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 git grep -E -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 536 | 2.670s (32.70x) |
./README.md:60:| [ack](https://github.com/beyondgrep/ack3) | `ack -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 2677 | 2.935s (35.94x) |
./README.md:61:
./README.md:62:Here's another benchmark on the same corpus as above that disregards gitignore
./README.md:63:files and searches with a whitelist instead. The corpus is the same as in the
./README.md:64:previous benchmark, and the flags passed to each command ensure that they are
./README.md:65:doing equivalent work:
./README.md:66:
./README.md:67:| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
./README.md:68:| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
./README.md:69:| ripgrep | `rg -uuu -tc -n -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | **0.063s** (1.00x) |
./README.md:70:| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.607s (9.62x) |
./README.md:71:| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `grep -E -r -n --include='*.c' --include='*.h' -w '[A-Z]+_SUSPEND'` | 447 | 0.674s (10.69x) |
./README.md:72:
./README.md:73:Now we'll move to searching on single large file. Here is a straight-up
./README.md:74:comparison between ripgrep, ugrep and GNU grep on a file cached in memory
./README.md:75:(~13GB, [`OpenSubtitles.raw.en.gz`](https://object.pouta.csc.fi/OPUS-OpenSubtitles/v2018/mono/en.txt.gz), decompressed):
./README.md:76:
./README.md:77:| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
./README.md:78:| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
./README.md:79:| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | **1.042s** (1.00x) |
./README.md:80:| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 1.339s (1.28x) |
./README.md:81:| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 egrep -w 'Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 7882 | 6.577s (6.31x) |
./README.md:82:
./README.md:83:In the above benchmark, passing the `-n` flag (for showing line numbers)
./README.md:84:increases the times to `1.664s` for ripgrep and `9.484s` for GNU grep. ugrep
./README.md:85:times are unaffected by the presence or absence of `-n`.
./README.md:86:
./README.md:87:Beware of performance cliffs though:
./README.md:88:
./README.md:89:| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
./README.md:90:| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
./README.md:91:| ripgrep (Unicode) | `rg -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | **1.053s** (1.00x) |
./README.md:92:| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 grep -E -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 6.234s (5.92x) |
./README.md:93:| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -w '[A-Z]\w+ Sherlock [A-Z]\w+'` | 485 | 28.973s (27.51x) |
./README.md:94:
./README.md:95:And performance can drop precipitously across the board when searching big
./README.md:96:files for patterns without any opportunities for literal optimizations:
./README.md:97:
./README.md:98:| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
./README.md:99:| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
./README.md:100:| ripgrep | `rg '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | **15.569s** (1.00x) |
./README.md:101:| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep -E '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | 21.857s (1.40x) |
./README.md:102:| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=C grep -E '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6749 | 32.409s (2.08x) |
./README.md:103:| [GNU grep (Unicode)](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=en_US.UTF-8 grep -E '[A-Za-z]{30}'` | 6795 | 8m30s (32.74x) |
./README.md:104:
./README.md:105:Finally, high match counts also tend to both tank performance and smooth
./README.md:106:out the differences between tools (because performance is dominated by how
./README.md:107:quickly one can handle a match and not the algorithm used to detect the match,
./README.md:108:generally speaking):
./README.md:109:
./README.md:110:| Tool | Command | Line count | Time |
./README.md:111:| ---- | ------- | ---------- | ---- |
./README.md:112:| ripgrep | `rg the` | 83499915 | **6.948s** (1.00x) |
./README.md:113:| [ugrep](https://github.com/Genivia/ugrep) | `ugrep the` | 83499915 | 11.721s (1.69x) |
./README.md:114:| [GNU grep](https://www.gnu.org/software/grep/) | `LC_ALL=C grep the` | 83499915 | 15.217s (2.19x) |
./README.md:115:
./README.md:116:### Why should I use ripgrep?
./README.md:117:
./README.md:118:* It can replace many use cases served by other search tools
./README.md:119:  because it contains most of their features and is generally faster. (See
./README.md:120:  [the FAQ](FAQ.md#posix4ever) for more details on whether ripgrep can truly
./README.md:121:  replace grep.)
./README.md:122:* Like other tools specialized to code search, ripgrep defaults to
./README.md:123:  [recursive search](GUIDE.md#recursive-search) and does [automatic
./README.md:124:  filtering](GUIDE.md#automatic-filtering). Namely, ripgrep won't search files
./README.md:125:  ignored by your `.gitignore`/`.ignore`/`.rgignore` files, it won't search
./README.md:126:  hidden files and it won't search binary files. Automatic filtering can be
./README.md:127:  disabled with `rg -uuu`.
./README.md:128:* ripgrep can [search specific types of files](GUIDE.md#manual-filtering-file-types).
./README.md:129:  For example, `rg -tpy foo` limits your search to Python files and `rg -Tjs
./README.md:130:  foo` excludes JavaScript files from your search. ripgrep can be taught about
./README.md:131:  new file types with custom matching rules.
./README.md:132:* ripgrep supports many features found in `grep`, such as showing the context
./README.md:133:  of search results, searching multiple patterns, highlighting matches with
./README.md:134:  color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, ripgrep stays fast while
./README.md:135:  supporting Unicode (which is always on).
./README.md:136:* ripgrep has optional support for switching its regex engine to use PCRE2.
./README.md:137:  Among other things, this makes it possible to use look-around and
./README.md:138:  backreferences in your patterns, which are not supported in ripgrep's default
./README.md:139:  regex engine. PCRE2 support can be enabled with `-P/--pcre2` (use PCRE2
./README.md:140:  always) or `--auto-hybrid-regex` (use PCRE2 only if needed). An alternative
./README.md:141:  syntax is provided via the `--engine (default|pcre2|auto)` option.
./README.md:142:* ripgrep has [rudimentary support for replacements](GUIDE.md#replacements),
./README.md:143:  which permit rewriting output based on what was matched.
./README.md:144:* ripgrep supports [searching files in text encodings](GUIDE.md#file-encoding)
./README.md:145:  other than UTF-8, such as UTF-16, latin-1, GBK, EUC-JP, Shift_JIS and more.
./README.md:146:  (Some support for automatically detecting UTF-16 is provided. Other text
./README.md:147:  encodings must be specifically specified with the `-E/--encoding` flag.)
./README.md:148:* ripgrep supports searching files compressed in a common format (brotli,
./README.md:149:  bzip2, gzip, lz4, lzma, xz, or zstandard) with the `-z/--search-zip` flag.
./README.md:150:* ripgrep supports
./README.md:151:  [arbitrary input preprocessing filters](GUIDE.md#preprocessor)
./README.md:152:  which could be PDF text extraction, less supported decompression, decrypting,
./README.md:153:  automatic encoding detection and so on.
./README.md:154:* ripgrep can be configured via a
./README.md:155:  [configuration file](GUIDE.md#configuration-file).
./README.md:156:
./README.md:157:In other words, use ripgrep if you like speed, filtering by default, fewer
./README.md:158:bugs and Unicode support.
./README.md:159:
./README.md:160:
./README.md:161:### Why shouldn't I use ripgrep?
./README.md:162:
./README.md:163:Despite initially not wanting to add every feature under the sun to ripgrep,
./README.md:164:over time, ripgrep has grown support for most features found in other file
./README.md:165:searching tools. This includes searching for results spanning across multiple
./README.md:166:lines, and opt-in support for PCRE2, which provides look-around and
./README.md:167:backreference support.
./README.md:168:
./README.md:169:At this point, the primary reasons not to use ripgrep probably consist of one
./README.md:170:or more of the following:
./README.md:171:
./README.md:172:* You need a portable and ubiquitous tool. While ripgrep works on Windows,
./README.md:173:  macOS and Linux, it is not ubiquitous and it does not conform to any
./README.md:174:  standard such as POSIX. The best tool for this job is good old grep.
./README.md:175:* There still exists some other feature (or bug) not listed in this README that
./README.md:176:  you rely on that's in another tool that isn't in ripgrep.
./README.md:177:* There is a performance edge case where ripgrep doesn't do well where another
./README.md:178:  tool does do well. (Please file a bug report!)
./README.md:179:* ripgrep isn't possible to install on your machine or isn't available for your
./README.md:180:  platform. (Please file a bug report!)
./README.md:181:
./README.md:182:
./README.md:183:### Is it really faster than everything else?
./README.md:184:
./README.md:185:Generally, yes. A large number of benchmarks with detailed analysis for each is
./README.md:186:[available on my blog](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/).
./README.md:187:
./README.md:188:Summarizing, ripgrep is fast because:
./README.md:189:
./README.md:190:* It is built on top of
./README.md:191:  [Rust's regex engine](https://github.com/rust-lang/regex).
./README.md:192:  Rust's regex engine uses finite automata, SIMD and aggressive literal
./README.md:193:  optimizations to make searching very fast. (PCRE2 support can be opted into
./README.md:194:  with the `-P/--pcre2` flag.)
./README.md:195:* Rust's regex library maintains performance with full Unicode support by
./README.md:196:  building UTF-8 decoding directly into its deterministic finite automaton
./README.md:197:  engine.
./README.md:198:* It supports searching with either memory maps or by searching incrementally
./README.md:199:  with an intermediate buffer. The former is better for single files and the
./README.md:200:  latter is better for large directories. ripgrep chooses the best searching
./README.md:201:  strategy for you automatically.
./README.md:202:* Applies your ignore patterns in `.gitignore` files using a
./README.md:203:  [`RegexSet`](https://docs.rs/regex/1/regex/struct.RegexSet.html).
./README.md:204:  That means a single file path can be matched against multiple glob patterns
./README.md:205:  simultaneously.
./README.md:206:* It uses a lock-free parallel recursive directory iterator, courtesy of
./README.md:207:  [`crossbeam`](https://docs.rs/crossbeam) and
./README.md:208:  [`ignore`](https://docs.rs/ignore).
./README.md:209:
./README.md:210:
./README.md:211:### Feature comparison
./README.md:212:
./README.md:213:Andy Lester, author of [ack](https://beyondgrep.com/), has published an
./README.md:214:excellent table comparing the features of ack, ag, git-grep, GNU grep and
./README.md:215:ripgrep: https://beyondgrep.com/feature-comparison/
./README.md:216:
./README.md:217:Note that ripgrep has grown a few significant new features recently that
./README.md:218:are not yet present in Andy's table. This includes, but is not limited to,
./README.md:219:configuration files, passthru, support for searching compressed files,
./README.md:220:multiline search and opt-in fancy regex support via PCRE2.

./README.md:234:
./README.md:235:The binary name for ripgrep is `rg`.

./README.md:237:**[Archives of precompiled binaries for ripgrep are available for Windows,
./README.md:238:macOS and Linux.](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases)** Linux and

./README.md:240:mentioned below are advised to download one of these archives.

./README.md:430:If you're a **Rust programmer**, ripgrep can be installed with `cargo`.

./README.md:451:### Building
./README.md:452:
./README.md:453:ripgrep is written in Rust, so you'll need to grab a
./README.md:454:[Rust installation](https://www.rust-lang.org/) in order to compile it.
./README.md:455:ripgrep compiles with Rust 1.96.0 (stable) or newer. In general, ripgrep tracks
./README.md:456:the latest stable release of the Rust compiler.
./README.md:457:
./README.md:458:To build ripgrep:
./README.md:459:
./README.md:460:```
./README.md:461:$ git clone https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep
./README.md:462:$ cd ripgrep
./README.md:463:$ cargo build --release
./README.md:464:$ ./target/release/rg --version
./README.md:465:0.1.3
./README.md:466:```
./README.md:467:
./README.md:468:**NOTE:** In the past, ripgrep supported a `simd-accel` Cargo feature when
./README.md:469:using a Rust nightly compiler. This only benefited UTF-16 transcoding.
./README.md:470:Since it required unstable features, this build mode was prone to breakage.
./README.md:471:Because of that, support for it has been removed. If you want SIMD
./README.md:472:optimizations for UTF-16 transcoding, then you'll have to petition the
./README.md:473:[`encoding_rs`](https://github.com/hsivonen/encoding_rs) project to use stable
./README.md:474:APIs.
./README.md:475:
./README.md:476:Finally, optional PCRE2 support can be built with ripgrep by enabling the
./README.md:477:`pcre2` feature:
./README.md:478:
./README.md:479:```
./README.md:480:$ cargo build --release --features 'pcre2'
./README.md:481:```
./README.md:482:
./README.md:483:Enabling the PCRE2 feature works with a stable Rust compiler and will
./README.md:484:attempt to automatically find and link with your system's PCRE2 library via
./README.md:485:`pkg-config`. If one doesn't exist, then ripgrep will build PCRE2 from source
./README.md:486:using your system's C compiler and then statically link it into the final
./README.md:487:executable. Static linking can be forced even when there is an available PCRE2
./README.md:488:system library by either building ripgrep with the MUSL target or by setting
./README.md:489:`PCRE2_SYS_STATIC=1`.
./README.md:490:
./README.md:491:ripgrep can be built with the MUSL target on Linux by first installing the MUSL
./README.md:492:library on your system (consult your friendly neighborhood package manager).
./README.md:493:Then you just need to add MUSL support to your Rust toolchain and rebuild
./README.md:494:ripgrep, which yields a fully static executable:
./README.md:495:
./README.md:496:```
./README.md:497:$ rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
./README.md:498:$ cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl
./README.md:499:```
./README.md:500:
./README.md:501:Applying the `--features` flag from above works as expected. If you want to
./README.md:502:build a static executable with MUSL and with PCRE2, then you will need to have
./README.md:503:`musl-gcc` installed, which might be in a separate package from the actual
./README.md:504:MUSL library, depending on your Linux distribution.
