./FAQ.md:154:How can I get results in a consistent order? ./FAQ.md:155:

./FAQ.md:157:By default, ripgrep uses parallelism to execute its search because this makes ./FAQ.md:158:the search much faster on most modern systems. This in turn means that ripgrep ./FAQ.md:159:has a non-deterministic aspect to it, since the interleaving of threads during ./FAQ.md:160:the execution of the program is itself non-deterministic. This has the effect ./FAQ.md:161:of printing results in a somewhat arbitrary order, and this order can change ./FAQ.md:162:from run to run of ripgrep. ./FAQ.md:164:The only way to make the order of results consistent is to ask ripgrep to ./FAQ.md:165:sort the output. Currently, this will disable all parallelism. (On smaller ./FAQ.md:166:repositories, you might not notice much of a performance difference!) You ./FAQ.md:167:can achieve this with the `--sort path` flag. ./FAQ.md:169:There is more discussion on this topic here: ./FAQ.md:170:https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/152 ./FAQ.md:173:

./FAQ.md:174:How do I search files that aren't UTF-8? ./FAQ.md:175:

./FAQ.md:177:See the [guide's section on file encoding](GUIDE.md#file-encoding). ./FAQ.md:180:

./FAQ.md:181:How do I search compressed files? ./FAQ.md:182:

./FAQ.md:184:ripgrep's `-z/--search-zip` flag will cause it to search compressed files ./FAQ.md:185:automatically. Currently, this supports gzip, bzip2, xz, lzma, lz4, Brotli and ./FAQ.md:186:Zstd. Each of these requires the corresponding `gzip`, `bzip2`, `xz`, ./FAQ.md:187:`lz4`, `brotli` and `zstd` binaries to be installed on your system. (That is, ./FAQ.md:188:ripgrep does decompression by shelling out to another process.) ./FAQ.md:190:ripgrep currently does not search archive formats, so `*.tar.gz` files, for ./FAQ.md:191:example, are skipped. ./FAQ.md:194:

./FAQ.md:195:How do I search over multiple lines? ./FAQ.md:196:

./FAQ.md:198:The `-U/--multiline` flag enables ripgrep to report results that span over ./FAQ.md:199:multiple lines. ./FAQ.md:202:

./FAQ.md:203:How do I use lookaround and/or backreferences? ./FAQ.md:204:

./FAQ.md:206:ripgrep's default regex engine does not support lookaround or backreferences. ./FAQ.md:207:This is primarily because the default regex engine is implemented using finite ./FAQ.md:208:state machines in order to guarantee a linear worst case time complexity on all ./FAQ.md:209:inputs. Backreferences are not possible to implement in this paradigm, and ./FAQ.md:210:lookaround appears difficult to do efficiently. ./FAQ.md:212:However, ripgrep optionally supports using PCRE2 as the regex engine instead of ./FAQ.md:213:the default one based on finite state machines. You can enable PCRE2 with the ./FAQ.md:214:`-P/--pcre2` flag. For example, in the root of the ripgrep repo, you can easily ./FAQ.md:215:find all palindromes: ./FAQ.md:218:$ rg -P '(\w{10})\1' ./FAQ.md:219:tests/misc.rs ./FAQ.md:220:483: cmd.arg("--max-filesize").arg("44444444444444444444"); ./FAQ.md:221:globset/src/glob.rs ./FAQ.md:222:1206: matches!(match7, "a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a*a", "aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa"); ./FAQ.md:225:If your version of ripgrep doesn't support PCRE2, then you'll get an error ./FAQ.md:226:message when you try to use the `-P/--pcre2` flag: ./FAQ.md:229:$ rg -P '(\w{10})\1' ./FAQ.md:230:PCRE2 is not available in this build of ripgrep ./FAQ.md:233:Most of the releases distributed by the ripgrep project here on GitHub will ./FAQ.md:234:come bundled with PCRE2 enabled. If you installed ripgrep through a different ./FAQ.md:235:means (like your system's package manager), then please reach out to the ./FAQ.md:236:maintainer of that package to see whether it's possible to enable the PCRE2 ./FAQ.md:237:feature. ./FAQ.md:240:

./FAQ.md:241:How do I configure ripgrep's colors? ./FAQ.md:242:

./FAQ.md:244:ripgrep has two flags related to colors: ./FAQ.md:246:* `--color` controls *when* to use colors. ./FAQ.md:247:* `--colors` controls *which* colors to use. ./FAQ.md:249:The `--color` flag accepts one of the following possible values: `never`, ./FAQ.md:250:`auto`, `always` or `ansi`. The `auto` value is the default and will cause ./FAQ.md:251:ripgrep to only enable colors when it is printing to a terminal. But if you ./FAQ.md:252:pipe ripgrep to a file or some other process, then it will suppress colors. ./FAQ.md:254:The `--colors` flag is a bit more complicated. The general format is: ./FAQ.md:257:--colors '{type}:{attribute}:{value}' ./FAQ.md:260:* `{type}` should be one of `path`, `line`, `column` or `match`. Each of these ./FAQ.md:261: correspond to the four different types of things that ripgrep will add color ./FAQ.md:262: to in its output. Select the type whose color you want to change. ./FAQ.md:263:* `{attribute}` should be one of `fg`, `bg` or `style`, corresponding to ./FAQ.md:264: foreground color, background color, or miscellaneous styling (such as whether ./FAQ.md:265: to bold the output or not). ./FAQ.md:266:* `{value}` is determined by the value of `{attribute}`. If ./FAQ.md:267: `{attribute}` is `style`, then `{value}` should be one of `nobold`, ./FAQ.md:268: `bold`, `nointense`, `intense`, `nounderline`, `underline`, `noitalic` or ./FAQ.md:269: `italic`. If `{attribute}` is `fg` or `bg`, then `{value}` should be a color. ./FAQ.md:271:A color is specified by either one of eight of English names, a single 256-bit ./FAQ.md:272:number or an RGB triple (with over 16 million possible values, or "true ./FAQ.md:273:color"). ./FAQ.md:275:The color names are `red`, `blue`, `green`, `cyan`, `magenta`, `yellow`, ./FAQ.md:276:`white` or `black`. ./FAQ.md:278:A single 256-bit number is a value in the range 0-255 (inclusive). It can ./FAQ.md:279:either be in decimal format (e.g., `62`) or hexadecimal format (e.g., `0x3E`). ./FAQ.md:281:An RGB triple corresponds to three numbers (decimal or hexadecimal) separated ./FAQ.md:282:by commas. ./FAQ.md:284:As a special case, `--colors '{type}:none'` will clear all colors and styles ./FAQ.md:285:associated with `{type}`, which lets you start with a clean slate (instead of ./FAQ.md:286:building on top of ripgrep's default color settings). ./FAQ.md:288:Here's an example that highlights the matches with a nice blue background with ./FAQ.md:289:bolded white text: ./FAQ.md:292:$ rg somepattern \ ./FAQ.md:293: --colors 'match:none' \ ./FAQ.md:294: --colors 'match:bg:0x33,0x66,0xFF' \ ./FAQ.md:295: --colors 'match:fg:white' \ ./FAQ.md:296: --colors 'match:style:bold' ./FAQ.md:299:Colors are an ideal candidate to set in your ./FAQ.md:300:[configuration file](GUIDE.md#configuration-file). See the ./FAQ.md:301:[question on emulating The Silver Searcher's output style](#silver-searcher-output) ./FAQ.md:302:for an example specific to colors. ./FAQ.md:305:

./FAQ.md:306:How do I enable true colors on Windows? ./FAQ.md:307:

./FAQ.md:309:First, see the previous question's ./FAQ.md:310:[answer on configuring colors](#colors). ./FAQ.md:312:Secondly, coloring on Windows is a bit complicated. If you're using a terminal ./FAQ.md:313:like Cygwin, then it's likely true color support already works out of the box. ./FAQ.md:314:However, if you are using a normal Windows console (`cmd` or `PowerShell`) and ./FAQ.md:315:a version of Windows prior to 10, then there is no known way to get true ./FAQ.md:316:color support. If you are on Windows 10 and using a Windows console, then ./FAQ.md:317:true colors should work out of the box with one caveat: you might need to ./FAQ.md:318:clear ripgrep's default color settings first. That is, instead of this: ./FAQ.md:321:$ rg somepattern --colors 'match:fg:0x33,0x66,0xFF' ./FAQ.md:324:you should do this ./FAQ.md:327:$ rg somepattern --colors 'match:none' --colors 'match:fg:0x33,0x66,0xFF' ./FAQ.md:330:This is because ripgrep might set the default style for `match` to `bold`, and ./FAQ.md:331:it seems like Windows 10's VT100 support doesn't permit bold and true color ./FAQ.md:332:ANSI escapes to be used simultaneously. The work-around above will clear ./FAQ.md:333:ripgrep's default styling, allowing you to craft it exactly as desired. ./FAQ.md:336:

./FAQ.md:337:How do I stop ripgrep from messing up colors when I kill it? ./FAQ.md:338:

./FAQ.md:340:Type in `color` in cmd.exe (Command Prompt) and `echo -ne "\033[0m"` on ./FAQ.md:341:Unix-like systems to restore your original foreground color. ./FAQ.md:343:In PowerShell, you can add the following code to your profile which will ./FAQ.md:344:restore the original foreground color when `Reset-ForegroundColor` is called. ./FAQ.md:345:Including the `Set-Alias` line will allow you to call it with simply `color`. ./FAQ.md:347:```powershell ./FAQ.md:348:$OrigFgColor = $Host.UI.RawUI.ForegroundColor ./FAQ.md:349:function Reset-ForegroundColor { ./FAQ.md:350: $Host.UI.RawUI.ForegroundColor = $OrigFgColor ./FAQ.md:352:Set-Alias -Name color -Value Reset-ForegroundColor ./FAQ.md:355:PR [#187](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/187) fixed this, and it ./FAQ.md:356:was later deprecated in ./FAQ.md:357:[#281](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/281). A full explanation is ./FAQ.md:358:available ./FAQ.md:359:[here](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/281#issuecomment-269093893). ./FAQ.md:362:

./FAQ.md:363:Why does using a leading `/` on Windows fail? ./FAQ.md:364:

./FAQ.md:366:If you're using cygwin on Windows and try to search for a pattern beginning ./FAQ.md:367:with a `/`, then it's possible that cygwin is mangling that pattern without ./FAQ.md:368:your knowledge. For example, if you tried running `rg /foo` in a cygwin shell ./FAQ.md:369:on Windows, then cygwin might mistakenly perform path translation on `/foo`, ./FAQ.md:370:which would result in `rg C:/msys64/foo` being searched instead. ./FAQ.md:372:You can fix this in one of three ways: ./FAQ.md:374:1. Stop using cygwin. ./FAQ.md:375:2. Escape the leading slash with an additional slash. e.g., `rg //foo`. ./FAQ.md:376:3. Temporarily disable path translation by setting `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1`. e.g., ./FAQ.md:377: `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 rg /foo`. ./FAQ.md:379:For more details, see https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1277 ./FAQ.md:382:

./FAQ.md:383:How do I get around the regex size limit? ./FAQ.md:384:

./FAQ.md:386:If you've given ripgrep a particularly large pattern (or a large number of ./FAQ.md:387:smaller patterns), then it is possible that it will fail to compile because it ./FAQ.md:388:hit a pre-set limit. For example: ./FAQ.md:391:$ rg '\pL{1000}' ./FAQ.md:392:Compiled regex exceeds size limit of 10485760 bytes. ./FAQ.md:395:(Note: `\pL{1000}` may look small, but `\pL` is the character class containing ./FAQ.md:396:all Unicode letters, which is quite large. *And* it's repeated 1000 times.) ./FAQ.md:398:In this case, you can work around by simply increasing the limit: ./FAQ.md:401:$ rg '\pL{1000}' --regex-size-limit 1G ./FAQ.md:404:Increasing the limit to 1GB does not necessarily mean that ripgrep will use ./FAQ.md:405:that much memory. The limit just says that it's allowed to (approximately) use ./FAQ.md:406:that much memory for constructing the regular expression. ./FAQ.md:409:

./FAQ.md:410:How do I make the -f/--file flag faster? ./FAQ.md:411:

./FAQ.md:413:The `-f/--file` permits one to give a file to ripgrep which contains a pattern ./FAQ.md:414:on each line. ripgrep will then report any line that matches any of the ./FAQ.md:415:patterns. ./FAQ.md:417:If this pattern file gets too big, then it is possible ripgrep will slow down ./FAQ.md:418:dramatically. *Typically* this is because an internal cache is too small, and ./FAQ.md:419:will cause ripgrep to spill over to a slower but more robust regular expression ./FAQ.md:420:engine. If this is indeed the problem, then it is possible to increase this ./FAQ.md:421:cache and regain speed. The cache can be controlled via the `--dfa-size-limit` ./FAQ.md:422:flag. For example, using `--dfa-size-limit 1G` will set the cache size to 1GB. ./FAQ.md:423:(Note that this doesn't mean ripgrep will use 1GB of memory automatically, but ./FAQ.md:424:it will allow the regex engine to if it needs to.) ./FAQ.md:427:

./FAQ.md:428:How do I make the output look like The Silver Searcher's output? ./FAQ.md:429:

./FAQ.md:431:Use the `--colors` flag, like so: ./FAQ.md:434:rg --colors line:fg:yellow \ ./FAQ.md:435: --colors line:style:bold \ ./FAQ.md:436: --colors path:fg:green \ ./FAQ.md:437: --colors path:style:bold \ ./FAQ.md:438: --colors match:fg:black \ ./FAQ.md:439: --colors match:bg:yellow \ ./FAQ.md:440: --colors match:style:nobold \ ./FAQ.md:441: foo ./FAQ.md:444:Alternatively, add your color configuration to your ripgrep config file (which ./FAQ.md:445:is activated by setting the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to point ./FAQ.md:446:to your config file). For example: ./FAQ.md:449:$ cat $HOME/.config/ripgrep/rc ./FAQ.md:450:--colors=line:fg:yellow ./FAQ.md:451:--colors=line:style:bold ./FAQ.md:452:--colors=path:fg:green ./FAQ.md:453:--colors=path:style:bold ./FAQ.md:454:--colors=match:fg:black ./FAQ.md:455:--colors=match:bg:yellow ./FAQ.md:456:--colors=match:style:nobold ./FAQ.md:457:$ RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH=$HOME/.config/ripgrep/rc rg foo ./FAQ.md:461:

./FAQ.md:462:Why does ripgrep get slower when I enable PCRE2 regexes? ./FAQ.md:463:

./FAQ.md:465:When you use the `--pcre2` (`-P` for short) flag, ripgrep will use the PCRE2 ./FAQ.md:466:regex engine instead of the default. Both regex engines are quite fast, ./FAQ.md:467:but PCRE2 provides a number of additional features such as look-around and ./FAQ.md:468:backreferences that many enjoy using. This is largely because PCRE2 uses ./FAQ.md:469:a backtracking implementation where as the default regex engine uses a finite ./FAQ.md:470:automaton based implementation. The former provides the ability to add lots of ./FAQ.md:471:bells and whistles over the latter, but the latter executes with worst case ./FAQ.md:472:linear time complexity. ./FAQ.md:474:With that out of the way, if you've used `-P` with ripgrep, you may have ./FAQ.md:475:noticed that it can be slower. The reasons for why this is are quite complex, ./FAQ.md:476:and they are complex because the optimizations that ripgrep uses to implement ./FAQ.md:477:fast search are complex. ./FAQ.md:479:The task ripgrep has before it is somewhat simple; all it needs to do is search ./FAQ.md:480:a file for occurrences of some pattern and then print the lines containing ./FAQ.md:481:those occurrences. The problem lies in what is considered a valid match and how ./FAQ.md:482:exactly we read the bytes from a file. ./FAQ.md:484:In terms of what is considered a valid match, remember that ripgrep will only ./FAQ.md:485:report matches spanning a single line by default. The problem here is that ./FAQ.md:486:some patterns can match across multiple lines, and ripgrep needs to prevent ./FAQ.md:487:that from happening. For example, `foo\sbar` will match `foo\nbar`. The most ./FAQ.md:488:obvious way to achieve this is to read the data from a file, and then apply ./FAQ.md:489:the pattern search to that data for each line. The problem with this approach ./FAQ.md:490:is that it can be quite slow; it would be much faster to let the pattern ./FAQ.md:491:search across as much data as possible. It's faster because it gets rid of the ./FAQ.md:492:overhead of finding the boundaries of every line, and also because it gets rid ./FAQ.md:493:of the overhead of starting and stopping the pattern search for every single ./FAQ.md:494:line. (This is operating under the general assumption that matching lines are ./FAQ.md:495:much rarer than non-matching lines.) ./FAQ.md:497:It turns out that we can use the faster approach by applying a very simple ./FAQ.md:498:restriction to the pattern: *statically prevent* the pattern from matching ./FAQ.md:499:through a `\n` character. Namely, when given a pattern like `foo\sbar`, ./FAQ.md:500:ripgrep will remove `\n` from the `\s` character class automatically. In some ./FAQ.md:501:cases, a simple removal is not so easy. For example, ripgrep will return an ./FAQ.md:502:error when your pattern includes a `\n` literal: ./FAQ.md:505:$ rg '\n' ./FAQ.md:506:the literal '"\n"' is not allowed in a regex ./FAQ.md:509:So what does this have to do with PCRE2? Well, ripgrep's default regex engine ./FAQ.md:510:exposes APIs for doing syntactic analysis on the pattern in a way that makes ./FAQ.md:511:it quite easy to strip `\n` from the pattern (or otherwise detect it and report ./FAQ.md:512:an error if stripping isn't possible). PCRE2 seemingly does not provide a ./FAQ.md:513:similar API, so ripgrep does not do any stripping when PCRE2 is enabled. This ./FAQ.md:514:forces ripgrep to use the "slow" search strategy of searching each line ./FAQ.md:515:individually. ./FAQ.md:517:OK, so if enabling PCRE2 slows down the default method of searching because it ./FAQ.md:518:forces matches to be limited to a single line, then why is PCRE2 also sometimes ./FAQ.md:519:slower when performing multiline searches? Well, that's because there are ./FAQ.md:520:*multiple* reasons why using PCRE2 in ripgrep can be slower than the default ./FAQ.md:521:regex engine. This time, blame PCRE2's Unicode support, which ripgrep enables ./FAQ.md:522:by default. In particular, PCRE2 cannot simultaneously enable Unicode support ./FAQ.md:523:and search arbitrary data. That is, when PCRE2's Unicode support is enabled, ./FAQ.md:524:the data **must** be valid UTF-8 (to do otherwise is to invoke undefined ./FAQ.md:525:behavior). This is in contrast to ripgrep's default regex engine, which can ./FAQ.md:526:enable Unicode support and still search arbitrary data. ripgrep's default ./FAQ.md:527:regex engine simply won't match invalid UTF-8 for a pattern that can otherwise ./FAQ.md:528:only match valid UTF-8. Why doesn't PCRE2 do the same? This author isn't ./FAQ.md:529:familiar with its internals, so we can't comment on it here. ./FAQ.md:531:The bottom line here is that we can't enable PCRE2's Unicode support without ./FAQ.md:532:simultaneously incurring a performance penalty for ensuring that we are ./FAQ.md:533:searching valid UTF-8. In particular, ripgrep will transcode the contents ./FAQ.md:534:of each file to UTF-8 while replacing invalid UTF-8 data with the Unicode ./FAQ.md:535:replacement codepoint. ripgrep then disables PCRE2's own internal UTF-8 ./FAQ.md:536:checking, since we've guaranteed the data we hand it will be valid UTF-8. The ./FAQ.md:537:reason why ripgrep takes this approach is because if we do hand PCRE2 invalid ./FAQ.md:538:UTF-8, then it will report a match error if it comes across an invalid UTF-8 ./FAQ.md:539:sequence. This is not good news for ripgrep, since it will stop it from ./FAQ.md:540:searching the rest of the file, and will also print potentially undesirable ./FAQ.md:541:error messages to users. ./FAQ.md:543:All right, the above is a lot of information to swallow if you aren't already ./FAQ.md:544:familiar with ripgrep internals. Let's make this concrete with some examples. ./FAQ.md:545:First, let's get some data big enough to magnify the performance differences: ./FAQ.md:548:$ curl -O 'https://burntsushi.net/stuff/subtitles2016-sample.gz' ./FAQ.md:549:$ gzip -d subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:550:$ md5sum subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:551:e3cb796a20bbc602fbfd6bb43bda45f5 subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:554:To search this data, we will use the pattern `^\w{42}$`, which contains exactly ./FAQ.md:555:one hit in the file and has no literals. Having no literals is important, ./FAQ.md:556:because it ensures that the regex engine won't use literal optimizations to ./FAQ.md:557:speed up the search. In other words, it lets us reason coherently about the ./FAQ.md:558:actual task that the regex engine is performing. ./FAQ.md:560:Let's now walk through a few examples in light of the information above. First, ./FAQ.md:561:let's consider the default search using ripgrep's default regex engine and ./FAQ.md:562:then the same search with PCRE2: ./FAQ.md:565:$ time rg '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:566:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:568:real 0m1.783s ./FAQ.md:569:user 0m1.731s ./FAQ.md:570:sys 0m0.051s ./FAQ.md:572:$ time rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:573:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:575:real 0m2.458s ./FAQ.md:576:user 0m2.419s ./FAQ.md:577:sys 0m0.038s ./FAQ.md:580:In this particular example, both pattern searches are using a Unicode aware ./FAQ.md:581:`\w` character class and both are counting lines in order to report line ./FAQ.md:582:numbers. The key difference here is that the first search will not search ./FAQ.md:583:line by line, but the second one will. We can observe which strategy ripgrep ./FAQ.md:584:uses by passing the `--trace` flag: ./FAQ.md:587:$ rg '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --trace ./FAQ.md:588:[... snip ...] ./FAQ.md:589:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:622: Some("subtitles2016-sample"): searching via memory map ./FAQ.md:590:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:712: slice reader: searching via slice-by-line strategy ./FAQ.md:591:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher::core|grep-searcher/src/searcher/core.rs:61: searcher core: will use fast line searcher ./FAQ.md:592:[... snip ...] ./FAQ.md:594:$ rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --trace ./FAQ.md:595:[... snip ...] ./FAQ.md:596:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:622: Some("subtitles2016-sample"): searching via memory map ./FAQ.md:597:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:705: slice reader: needs transcoding, using generic reader ./FAQ.md:598:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher|grep-searcher/src/searcher/mod.rs:685: generic reader: searching via roll buffer strategy ./FAQ.md:599:TRACE|grep_searcher::searcher::core|grep-searcher/src/searcher/core.rs:63: searcher core: will use slow line searcher ./FAQ.md:600:[... snip ...] ./FAQ.md:603:The first says it is using the "fast line searcher" where as the latter says ./FAQ.md:604:it is using the "slow line searcher." The latter also shows that we are ./FAQ.md:605:decoding the contents of the file, which also impacts performance. ./FAQ.md:607:Interestingly, in this case, the pattern does not match a `\n` and the file ./FAQ.md:608:we're searching is valid UTF-8, so neither the slow line-by-line search ./FAQ.md:609:strategy nor the decoding are necessary. We could fix the former issue with ./FAQ.md:610:better PCRE2 introspection APIs. We can actually fix the latter issue with ./FAQ.md:611:ripgrep's `--no-encoding` flag, which prevents the automatic UTF-8 decoding, ./FAQ.md:612:but will enable PCRE2's own UTF-8 validity checking. Unfortunately, it's slower ./FAQ.md:613:in my build of ripgrep: ./FAQ.md:616:$ time rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --no-encoding ./FAQ.md:617:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:619:real 0m3.074s ./FAQ.md:620:user 0m3.021s ./FAQ.md:621:sys 0m0.051s ./FAQ.md:624:(Tip: use the `--trace` flag to verify that no decoding in ripgrep is ./FAQ.md:625:happening.) ./FAQ.md:627:A possible reason why PCRE2's UTF-8 checking is slower is because it might ./FAQ.md:628:not be better than the highly optimized UTF-8 checking routines found in the ./FAQ.md:629:[`encoding_rs`](https://github.com/hsivonen/encoding_rs) library, which is what ./FAQ.md:630:ripgrep uses for UTF-8 decoding. Moreover, my build of ripgrep enables ./FAQ.md:631:`encoding_rs`'s SIMD optimizations, which may be in play here. ./FAQ.md:633:Also, note that using the `--no-encoding` flag can cause PCRE2 to report ./FAQ.md:634:invalid UTF-8 errors, which causes ripgrep to stop searching the file: ./FAQ.md:637:$ cat invalid-utf8 ./FAQ.md:638:foobar ./FAQ.md:640:$ xxd invalid-utf8 ./FAQ.md:641:00000000: 666f 6fff 6261 720a foo.bar. ./FAQ.md:643:$ rg foo invalid-utf8 ./FAQ.md:644:1:foobar ./FAQ.md:646:$ rg -P foo invalid-utf8 ./FAQ.md:647:1:foo�bar ./FAQ.md:649:$ rg -P foo invalid-utf8 --no-encoding ./FAQ.md:650:invalid-utf8: PCRE2: error matching: UTF-8 error: illegal byte (0xfe or 0xff) ./FAQ.md:653:All right, so at this point, you might think that we could remove the penalty ./FAQ.md:654:for line-by-line searching by enabling multiline search. After all, our ./FAQ.md:655:particular pattern can't match across multiple lines anyway, so we'll still get ./FAQ.md:656:the results we want. Let's try it: ./FAQ.md:659:$ time rg -U '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:660:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:662:real 0m1.803s ./FAQ.md:663:user 0m1.748s ./FAQ.md:664:sys 0m0.054s ./FAQ.md:666:$ time rg -P -U '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:667:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:669:real 0m2.962s ./FAQ.md:670:user 0m2.246s ./FAQ.md:671:sys 0m0.713s ./FAQ.md:674:Search times remain the same with the default regex engine, but the PCRE2 ./FAQ.md:675:search gets _slower_. What happened? The secrets can be revealed with the ./FAQ.md:676:`--trace` flag once again. In the former case, ripgrep actually detects that ./FAQ.md:677:the pattern can't match across multiple lines, and so will fall back to the ./FAQ.md:678:"fast line search" strategy as with our search without `-U`. ./FAQ.md:680:However, for PCRE2, things are much worse. Namely, since Unicode mode is still ./FAQ.md:681:enabled, ripgrep is still going to decode UTF-8 to ensure that it hands only ./FAQ.md:682:valid UTF-8 to PCRE2. Unfortunately, one key downside of multiline search is ./FAQ.md:683:that ripgrep cannot do it incrementally. Since matches can be arbitrarily long, ./FAQ.md:684:ripgrep actually needs the entire file in memory at once. Normally, we can use ./FAQ.md:685:a memory map for this, but because we need to UTF-8 decode the file before ./FAQ.md:686:searching it, ripgrep winds up reading the entire contents of the file on to ./FAQ.md:687:the heap before executing a search. Owch. ./FAQ.md:689:OK, so Unicode is killing us here. The file we're searching is _mostly_ ASCII, ./FAQ.md:690:so maybe we're OK with missing some data. (Try `rg '[\w--\p{ascii}]'` to see ./FAQ.md:691:non-ASCII word characters that an ASCII-only `\w` character class would miss.) ./FAQ.md:692:We can disable Unicode in both searches, but this is done differently depending ./FAQ.md:693:on the regex engine we use: ./FAQ.md:696:$ time rg '(?-u)^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:697:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:699:real 0m1.714s ./FAQ.md:700:user 0m1.669s ./FAQ.md:701:sys 0m0.044s ./FAQ.md:703:$ time rg -P '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --no-pcre2-unicode ./FAQ.md:704:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:706:real 0m1.997s ./FAQ.md:707:user 0m1.958s ./FAQ.md:708:sys 0m0.037s ./FAQ.md:711:For the most part, ripgrep's default regex engine performs about the same. ./FAQ.md:712:PCRE2 does improve a little bit, and is now almost as fast as the default ./FAQ.md:713:regex engine. If you look at the output of `--trace`, you'll see that ripgrep ./FAQ.md:714:will no longer perform UTF-8 decoding, but it does still use the slow ./FAQ.md:715:line-by-line searcher. ./FAQ.md:717:At this point, we can combine all of our insights above: let's try to get off ./FAQ.md:718:of the slow line-by-line searcher by enabling multiline mode, and let's stop ./FAQ.md:719:UTF-8 decoding by disabling Unicode support: ./FAQ.md:722:$ time rg -U '(?-u)^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample ./FAQ.md:723:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:725:real 0m1.714s ./FAQ.md:726:user 0m1.655s ./FAQ.md:727:sys 0m0.058s ./FAQ.md:729:$ time rg -P -U '^\w{42}$' subtitles2016-sample --no-pcre2-unicode ./FAQ.md:730:21225780:EverymajordevelopmentinthehistoryofAmerica ./FAQ.md:732:real 0m1.121s ./FAQ.md:733:user 0m1.071s ./FAQ.md:734:sys 0m0.048s ./FAQ.md:737:Ah, there's PCRE2's JIT shining! ripgrep's default regex engine once again ./FAQ.md:738:remains about the same, but PCRE2 no longer needs to search line-by-line and it ./FAQ.md:739:no longer needs to do any kind of UTF-8 checks. This allows the file to get ./FAQ.md:740:memory mapped and passed right through PCRE2's JIT at impressive speeds. (As ./FAQ.md:741:a brief and interesting historical note, the configuration of "memory map + ./FAQ.md:742:multiline + no-Unicode" is exactly the configuration used by The Silver ./FAQ.md:743:Searcher. This analysis perhaps sheds some reasoning as to why that ./FAQ.md:744:configuration is useful!) ./FAQ.md:746:In summary, if you want PCRE2 to go as fast as possible and you don't care ./FAQ.md:747:about Unicode and you don't care about matches possibly spanning across ./FAQ.md:748:multiple lines, then enable multiline mode with `-U` and disable PCRE2's ./FAQ.md:749:Unicode support with the `--no-pcre2-unicode` flag. ./FAQ.md:751:Caveat emptor: This author is not a PCRE2 expert, so there may be APIs that can ./FAQ.md:752:improve performance that the author missed. Similarly, there may be alternative ./FAQ.md:753:designs for a searching tool that are more amenable to how PCRE2 works. ./FAQ.md:756:

./FAQ.md:833:How do I pipe non-ASCII content to ripgrep on Windows? ./FAQ.md:834:

./FAQ.md:860:How can I search and replace with ripgrep? ./FAQ.md:861:

./FAQ.md:863:Using ripgrep alone, you can't. ripgrep is a search tool that will never ./FAQ.md:864:touch your files. However, the output of ripgrep can be piped to other tools ./FAQ.md:865:that do modify files on disk. See ./FAQ.md:866:[this issue](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/74) for more ./FAQ.md:867:information. ./FAQ.md:869:sed is one such tool that can modify files on disk. sed can take a filename ./FAQ.md:870:and a substitution command to search and replace in the specified file. ./FAQ.md:871:Files containing matching patterns can be provided to sed using ./FAQ.md:874:rg foo --files-with-matches ./FAQ.md:877:The output of this command is a list of filenames that contain a match for ./FAQ.md:878:the `foo` pattern. ./FAQ.md:880:This list can be piped into `xargs`, which will split the filenames from ./FAQ.md:881:standard input into arguments for the command following xargs. You can use this ./FAQ.md:882:combination to pipe a list of filenames into sed for replacement. For example: ./FAQ.md:885:rg foo --files-with-matches | xargs sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' ./FAQ.md:888:will replace all instances of 'foo' with 'bar' in the files in which ./FAQ.md:889:ripgrep finds the foo pattern. The `-i` flag to sed indicates that you are ./FAQ.md:890:editing files in place, and `s/foo/bar/g` says that you are performing a ./FAQ.md:891:**s**ubstitution of the pattern `foo` for `bar`, and that you are doing this ./FAQ.md:892:substitution **g**lobally (all occurrences of the pattern in each file). ./FAQ.md:894:Note: the above command assumes that you are using GNU sed. If you are using ./FAQ.md:895:BSD sed (the default on macOS and FreeBSD) then you must modify the above ./FAQ.md:896:command to be the following: ./FAQ.md:899:rg foo --files-with-matches | xargs sed -i '' 's/foo/bar/g' ./FAQ.md:902:The `-i` flag in BSD sed requires a file extension to be given to make backups ./FAQ.md:903:for all modified files. Specifying the empty string prevents file backups from ./FAQ.md:904:being made. ./FAQ.md:906:Finally, if any of your file paths contain whitespace in them, then you might ./FAQ.md:907:need to delimit your file paths with a NUL terminator. This requires telling ./FAQ.md:908:ripgrep to output NUL bytes between each path, and telling xargs to read paths ./FAQ.md:909:delimited by NUL bytes: ./FAQ.md:912:rg foo --files-with-matches -0 | xargs -0 sed -i 's/foo/bar/g' ./FAQ.md:915:To learn more about sed, see the sed manual ./FAQ.md:916:[here](https://www.gnu.org/software/sed/manual/sed.html). ./FAQ.md:918:Additionally, Facebook has a tool called ./FAQ.md:919:[fastmod](https://github.com/facebookincubator/fastmod) ./FAQ.md:920:that uses some of the same libraries as ripgrep and might provide a more ./FAQ.md:921:ergonomic search-and-replace experience. ./FAQ.md:924:

./FAQ.md:953:Can ripgrep replace grep? ./FAQ.md:954:

./FAQ.md:956:Yes and no. ./FAQ.md:958:If, upon hearing that "ripgrep can replace grep," you *actually* hear, "ripgrep ./FAQ.md:959:can be used in every instance grep can be used, in exactly the same way, for ./FAQ.md:960:the same use cases, with exactly the same bug-for-bug behavior," then no, ./FAQ.md:961:ripgrep trivially *cannot* replace grep. Moreover, ripgrep will *never* replace ./FAQ.md:962:grep. ./FAQ.md:964:If, upon hearing that "ripgrep can replace grep," you *actually* hear, "ripgrep ./FAQ.md:965:can replace grep in some cases and not in other use cases," then yes, that is ./FAQ.md:966:indeed true! ./FAQ.md:968:Let's go over some of those use cases in favor of ripgrep. Some of these may ./FAQ.md:969:not apply to you. That's OK. There may be other use cases not listed here that ./FAQ.md:970:do apply to you. That's OK too. ./FAQ.md:972:(For all claims related to performance in the following words, see my ./FAQ.md:973:[blog post](https://blog.burntsushi.net/ripgrep/) ./FAQ.md:974:introducing ripgrep.) ./FAQ.md:976:* Are you frequently searching a repository of code? If so, ripgrep might be a ./FAQ.md:977: good choice since there's likely a good chunk of your repository that you ./FAQ.md:978: don't want to search. grep, can, of course, be made to filter files using ./FAQ.md:979: recursive search, and if you don't mind writing out the requisite `--exclude` ./FAQ.md:980: rules or writing wrapper scripts, then grep might be sufficient. (I'm not ./FAQ.md:981: kidding, I myself did this with grep for almost a decade before writing ./FAQ.md:982: ripgrep.) But if you instead enjoy having a search tool respect your ./FAQ.md:983: `.gitignore`, then ripgrep might be perfect for you! ./FAQ.md:984:* Are you frequently searching non-ASCII text that is UTF-8 encoded? One of ./FAQ.md:985: ripgrep's key features is that it can handle Unicode features in your ./FAQ.md:986: patterns in a way that tends to be faster than GNU grep. Unicode features ./FAQ.md:987: in ripgrep are enabled by default; there is no need to configure your locale ./FAQ.md:988: settings to use ripgrep properly because ripgrep doesn't respect your locale ./FAQ.md:989: settings. ./FAQ.md:990:* Do you need to search UTF-16 files and you don't want to bother explicitly ./FAQ.md:991: transcoding them? Great. ripgrep does this for you automatically. No need ./FAQ.md:992: to enable it. ./FAQ.md:993:* Do you need to search a large directory of large files? ripgrep uses ./FAQ.md:994: parallelism by default, which tends to make it faster than a standard ./FAQ.md:995: `grep -r` search. However, if you're OK writing the occasional ./FAQ.md:996: `find ./ -print0 | xargs -P8 -0 grep` command, then maybe grep is good ./FAQ.md:997: enough. ./FAQ.md:999:Here are some cases where you might *not* want to use ripgrep. The same caveats ./FAQ.md:1000:for the previous section apply. ./FAQ.md:1002:* Are you writing portable shell scripts intended to work in a variety of ./FAQ.md:1003: environments? Great, probably not a good idea to use ripgrep! ripgrep has ./FAQ.md:1004: nowhere near the ubiquity of grep, so if you do use ripgrep, you might need ./FAQ.md:1005: to futz with the installation process more than you would with grep. ./FAQ.md:1006:* Do you care about POSIX compatibility? If so, then you can't use ripgrep ./FAQ.md:1007: because it never was, isn't and never will be POSIX compatible. ./FAQ.md:1008:* Do you hate tools that try to do something smart? If so, ripgrep is all about ./FAQ.md:1009: being smart, so you might prefer to just stick with grep. ./FAQ.md:1010:* Is there a particular feature of grep you rely on that ripgrep either doesn't ./FAQ.md:1011: have or never will have? If the former, file a bug report, maybe ripgrep can ./FAQ.md:1012: do it! If the latter, well, then, just use grep. ./FAQ.md:1015:

./FAQ.md:1016:What does the "rip" in ripgrep mean? ./FAQ.md:1017:

./FAQ.md:1019:When I first started writing ripgrep, I called it `rep`, intending it to be a ./FAQ.md:1020:shorter variant of `grep`. Soon after, I renamed it to `xrep` since `rep` ./FAQ.md:1021:wasn't obvious enough of a name for my taste. And also because adding `x` to ./FAQ.md:1022:anything always makes it better, right? ./FAQ.md:1024:Before ripgrep's first public release, I decided that I didn't like `xrep`. I ./FAQ.md:1025:thought it was slightly awkward to type, and despite my previous praise of the ./FAQ.md:1026:letter `x`, I kind of thought it was pretty lame. Being someone who really ./FAQ.md:1027:likes Rust, I wanted to call it "rustgrep" or maybe "rgrep" for short. But I ./FAQ.md:1028:thought that was just as lame, and maybe a little too in-your-face. But I ./FAQ.md:1029:wanted to continue using `r` so I could at least pretend Rust had something to ./FAQ.md:1030:do with it. ./FAQ.md:1032:I spent a couple of days trying to think of very short words that began with ./FAQ.md:1033:the letter `r` that were even somewhat related to the task of searching. I ./FAQ.md:1034:don't remember how it popped into my head, but "rip" came up as something that ./FAQ.md:1035:meant "fast," as in, "to rip through your text." The fact that RIP is also ./FAQ.md:1036:an initialism for "Rest in Peace" (as in, "ripgrep kills grep") never really ./FAQ.md:1037:dawned on me. Perhaps the coincidence is too striking to believe that, but ./FAQ.md:1038:I didn't realize it until someone explicitly pointed it out to me after the ./FAQ.md:1039:initial public release. I admit that I found it mildly amusing, but if I had ./FAQ.md:1040:realized it myself before the public release, I probably would have pressed on ./FAQ.md:1041:and chose a different name. Alas, renaming things after a release is hard, so I ./FAQ.md:1042:decided to mush on. ./FAQ.md:1044:Given the fact that ./FAQ.md:1045:[ripgrep never was, is or will be a 100% drop-in replacement for ./FAQ.md:1046:grep](#posix4ever), ./FAQ.md:1047:ripgrep is neither actually a "grep killer" nor was it ever intended to be. It ./FAQ.md:1048:certainly does eat into some of its use cases, but that's nothing that other ./FAQ.md:1049:tools like ack or The Silver Searcher weren't already doing. ./FAQ.md:1052:

Notably, ./CHANGELOG.md:732:ripgrep's user experience for binary file filtering has been improved. See the ./CHANGELOG.md:733:[guide's new section on binary data](GUIDE.md#binary-data) for more details. ./CHANGELOG.md:735:This release also marks a change in ripgrep's versioning. Where as the previous ./CHANGELOG.md:736:version was `0.10.0`, this version is `11.0.0`. Moving forward, ripgrep's ./CHANGELOG.md:737:major version will be increased a few times per year. ripgrep will continue to ./CHANGELOG.md:738:be conservative with respect to backwards compatibility, but may occasionally ./CHANGELOG.md:739:introduce breaking changes, which will always be documented in this CHANGELOG. ./CHANGELOG.md:740:See [issue 1172](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/1172) for a bit ./CHANGELOG.md:741:more detail on why this versioning change was made. ./CHANGELOG.md:743:This release increases the **minimum supported Rust version** from 1.28.0 to ./CHANGELOG.md:744:1.34.0. ./CHANGELOG.md:746:**BREAKING CHANGES**: ./CHANGELOG.md:748:* ripgrep has tweaked its exit status codes to be more like GNU grep's. Namely, ./CHANGELOG.md:749: if a non-fatal error occurs during a search, then ripgrep will now always ./CHANGELOG.md:750: emit a `2` exit status code, regardless of whether a match is found or not. ./CHANGELOG.md:751: Previously, ripgrep would only emit a `2` exit status code for a catastrophic ./CHANGELOG.md:752: error (e.g., regex syntax error). One exception to this is if ripgrep is run ./CHANGELOG.md:753: with `-q/--quiet`. In that case, if an error occurs and a match is found, ./CHANGELOG.md:754: then ripgrep will exit with a `0` exit status code. ./CHANGELOG.md:755:* Supplying the `-u/--unrestricted` flag three times is now equivalent to ./CHANGELOG.md:756: supplying `--no-ignore --hidden --binary`. Previously, `-uuu` was equivalent ./CHANGELOG.md:757: to `--no-ignore --hidden --text`. The difference is that `--binary` disables ./CHANGELOG.md:758: binary file filtering without potentially dumping binary data into your ./CHANGELOG.md:759: terminal. That is, `rg -uuu foo` should now be equivalent to `grep -r foo`. ./CHANGELOG.md:760:* The `avx-accel` feature of ripgrep has been removed since it is no longer ./CHANGELOG.md:761: necessary. All uses of AVX in ripgrep are now enabled automatically via ./CHANGELOG.md:762: runtime CPU feature detection. The `simd-accel` feature does remain available ./CHANGELOG.md:763: (only for enabling SIMD for transcoding), however, it does increase ./CHANGELOG.md:764: compilation times substantially at the moment. ./CHANGELOG.md:766:Performance improvements: ./CHANGELOG.md:768:* [PERF #497](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/497), ./CHANGELOG.md:769: [PERF #838](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/838): ./CHANGELOG.md:770: Make `rg -F -f dictionary-of-literals` much faster. ./CHANGELOG.md:772:Feature enhancements: ./CHANGELOG.md:774:* Added or improved file type filtering for Apache Thrift, ASP, Bazel, Brotli, ./CHANGELOG.md:775: BuildStream, bzip2, C, C++, Cython, gzip, Java, Make, Postscript, QML, Tex, ./CHANGELOG.md:776: XML, xz, zig and zstd. ./CHANGELOG.md:777:* [FEATURE #855](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/855): ./CHANGELOG.md:778: Add `--binary` flag for disabling binary file filtering. ./CHANGELOG.md:779:* [FEATURE #1078](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/1078): ./CHANGELOG.md:780: Add `--max-columns-preview` flag for showing a preview of long lines. ./CHANGELOG.md:781:* [FEATURE #1099](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/1099): ./CHANGELOG.md:782: Add support for Brotli and Zstd to the `-z/--search-zip` flag. ./CHANGELOG.md:783:* [FEATURE #1138](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/1138): ./CHANGELOG.md:784: Add `--no-ignore-dot` flag for ignoring `.ignore` files. ./CHANGELOG.md:785:* [FEATURE #1155](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/1155): ./CHANGELOG.md:786: Add `--auto-hybrid-regex` flag for automatically falling back to PCRE2. ./CHANGELOG.md:787:* [FEATURE #1159](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/pull/1159): ./CHANGELOG.md:788: ripgrep's exit status logic should now match GNU grep. By default, when you search a directory, ripgrep will ignore all of ./GUIDE.md:178:the following: ./GUIDE.md:180:1. Files and directories that match glob patterns in these three categories: ./GUIDE.md:181: 1. `.gitignore` globs (including global and repo-specific globs). This ./GUIDE.md:182: includes `.gitignore` files in parent directories that are part of the ./GUIDE.md:183: same `git` repository. (Unless the `--no-require-git` flag is given.) ./GUIDE.md:184: 2. `.ignore` globs, which take precedence over all gitignore globs ./GUIDE.md:185: when there's a conflict. This includes `.ignore` files in parent ./GUIDE.md:186: directories. ./GUIDE.md:187: 3. `.rgignore` globs, which take precedence over all `.ignore` globs ./GUIDE.md:188: when there's a conflict. This includes `.rgignore` files in parent ./GUIDE.md:189: directories. ./GUIDE.md:190:2. Hidden files and directories. ./GUIDE.md:191:3. Binary files. (ripgrep considers any file with a `NUL` byte to be binary.) ./GUIDE.md:192:4. Symbolic links aren't followed. ./GUIDE.md:194:All of these things can be toggled using various flags provided by ripgrep: ./GUIDE.md:196:1. You can disable all ignore-related filtering with the `--no-ignore` flag. ./GUIDE.md:197:2. Hidden files and directories can be searched with the `--hidden` (`-.` for ./GUIDE.md:198:short) flag. ./GUIDE.md:199:3. Binary files can be searched via the `--text` (`-a` for short) flag. ./GUIDE.md:200: Be careful with this flag! Binary files may emit control characters to your ./GUIDE.md:201: terminal, which might cause strange behavior. ./GUIDE.md:202:4. ripgrep can follow symlinks with the `--follow` (`-L` for short) flag. ./GUIDE.md:204:As a special convenience, ripgrep also provides a flag called `--unrestricted` ./GUIDE.md:205:(`-u` for short). Repeated uses of this flag will cause ripgrep to disable ./GUIDE.md:206:more and more of its filtering. That is, `-u` will disable `.gitignore` ./GUIDE.md:207:handling, `-uu` will search hidden files and directories and `-uuu` will search ./GUIDE.md:208:binary files. This is useful when you're using ripgrep and you aren't sure ./GUIDE.md:209:whether its filtering is hiding results from you. Tacking on a couple `-u` ./GUIDE.md:210:flags is a quick way to find out. (Use the `--debug` flag if you're still ./GUIDE.md:211:perplexed, and if that doesn't help, ./GUIDE.md:212:[file an issue](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/issues/new).) ./GUIDE.md:214:ripgrep's `.gitignore` handling actually goes a bit beyond just `.gitignore` ./GUIDE.md:215:files. ripgrep will also respect repository specific rules found in ./GUIDE.md:216:`$GIT_DIR/info/exclude`, as well as any global ignore rules in your ./GUIDE.md:217:`core.excludesFile` (which is usually `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git/ignore` on ./GUIDE.md:218:Unix-like systems). ./GUIDE.md:220:Sometimes you want to search files that are in your `.gitignore`, so it is ./GUIDE.md:221:possible to specify additional ignore rules or overrides in a `.ignore` ./GUIDE.md:222:(application agnostic) or `.rgignore` (ripgrep specific) file. ./GUIDE.md:224:For example, let's say you have a `.gitignore` file that looks like this: ./GUIDE.md:227:log/ ./GUIDE.md:230:This generally means that any `log` directory won't be tracked by `git`. ./GUIDE.md:231:However, perhaps it contains useful output that you'd like to include in your ./GUIDE.md:232:searches, but you still don't want to track it in `git`. Note though that this can come ./GUIDE.md:252:with a significant performance penalty, and is therefore disabled by default. ./GUIDE.md:254:For a more in depth description of how glob patterns in a `.gitignore` file ./GUIDE.md:255:are interpreted, please see `man gitignore`. ./GUIDE.md:258:### Manual filtering: globs ./GUIDE.md:260:In the previous section, we talked about ripgrep's filtering that it does by ./GUIDE.md:261:default. It is "automatic" because it reacts to your environment. That is, it ./GUIDE.md:262:uses already existing `.gitignore` files to produce more relevant search ./GUIDE.md:263:results. ./GUIDE.md:265:In addition to automatic filtering, ripgrep also provides more manual or ad hoc ./GUIDE.md:266:filtering. This comes in two varieties: additional glob patterns specified in ./GUIDE.md:267:your ripgrep commands and file type filtering. This section covers glob ./GUIDE.md:268:patterns while the next section covers file type filtering. ./GUIDE.md:270:In our ripgrep source code (see [Basics](#basics) for instructions on how to ./GUIDE.md:271:get a source archive to search), let's say we wanted to see which things depend ./GUIDE.md:272:on `lexopt`, our argument parser. ./GUIDE.md:274:We could do this: ./GUIDE.md:277:$ rg lexopt ./GUIDE.md:278:[lots of results] ./GUIDE.md:281:But this shows us many things, and we're only interested in where we wrote ./GUIDE.md:282:`lexopt` as a dependency. Instead, we could limit ourselves to TOML files, ./GUIDE.md:283:which is how dependencies are communicated to Rust's build tool, Cargo: ./GUIDE.md:286:$ rg lexopt -g '*.toml' ./GUIDE.md:287:Cargo.toml ./GUIDE.md:288:57:lexopt = "0.3.0" ./GUIDE.md:291:The `-g '*.toml'` syntax says, "make sure every file searched matches this ./GUIDE.md:292:glob pattern." Note that we put `'*.toml'` in single quotes to prevent our ./GUIDE.md:293:shell from expanding the `*`. ./GUIDE.md:295:If we wanted, we could tell ripgrep to search anything *but* `*.toml` files: ./GUIDE.md:298:$ rg lexopt -g '!*.toml' ./GUIDE.md:299:[lots of results] ./GUIDE.md:302:This will give you a lot of results again as above, but they won't include ./GUIDE.md:303:files ending with `.toml`. Note that the use of a `!` here to mean "negation" ./GUIDE.md:304:is a bit non-standard, but it was chosen to be consistent with how globs in ./GUIDE.md:305:`.gitignore` files are written. (Although, the meaning is reversed. In ./GUIDE.md:306:`.gitignore` files, a `!` prefix means whitelist, and on the command line, a ./GUIDE.md:307:`!` means blacklist.) ./GUIDE.md:309:Globs are interpreted in exactly the same way as `.gitignore` patterns. That ./GUIDE.md:310:is, later globs will override earlier globs. For example, the following command ./GUIDE.md:311:will search only `*.toml` files: ./GUIDE.md:314:$ rg lexopt -g '!*.toml' -g '*.toml' ./GUIDE.md:317:Interestingly, reversing the order of the globs in this case will match ./GUIDE.md:318:nothing, since the presence of at least one non-blacklist glob will institute a ./GUIDE.md:319:requirement that every file searched must match at least one glob. In this ./GUIDE.md:320:case, the blacklist glob takes precedence over the previous glob and prevents ./GUIDE.md:321:any file from being searched at all! ./GUIDE.md:324:### Manual filtering: file types ./GUIDE.md:326:Over time, you might notice that you use the same glob patterns over and over. ./GUIDE.md:327:For example, you might find yourself doing a lot of searches where you only ./GUIDE.md:328:want to see results for Rust files: ./GUIDE.md:331:$ rg 'fn run' -g '*.rs' ./GUIDE.md:334:Instead of writing out the glob every time, you can use ripgrep's support for ./GUIDE.md:335:file types: ./GUIDE.md:338:$ rg 'fn run' --type rust ./GUIDE.md:341:or, more succinctly, ./GUIDE.md:344:$ rg 'fn run' -trust ./GUIDE.md:347:The way the `--type` flag functions is simple. It acts as a name that is ./GUIDE.md:348:assigned to one or more globs that match the relevant files. This lets you ./GUIDE.md:349:write a single type that might encompass a broad range of file extensions. For ./GUIDE.md:350:example, if you wanted to search C files, you'd have to check both C source ./GUIDE.md:351:files and C header files: ./GUIDE.md:354:$ rg 'int main' -g '*.{c,h}' ./GUIDE.md:357:or you could just use the C file type: ./GUIDE.md:360:$ rg 'int main' -tc ./GUIDE.md:363:Just as you can write blacklist globs, you can blacklist file types too: ./GUIDE.md:366:$ rg lexopt --type-not rust ./GUIDE.md:369:or, more succinctly, ./GUIDE.md:372:$ rg lexopt -Trust ./GUIDE.md:375:That is, `-t` means "include files of this type" where as `-T` means "exclude ./GUIDE.md:376:files of this type." ./GUIDE.md:378:To see the globs that make up a type, run `rg --type-list`: ./GUIDE.md:381:$ rg --type-list | rg '^make:' ./GUIDE.md:382:make: *.mak, *.mk, GNUmakefile, Gnumakefile, Makefile, gnumakefile, makefile ./GUIDE.md:385:By default, ripgrep comes with a bunch of pre-defined types. Generally, these ./GUIDE.md:386:types correspond to well known public formats. But you can define your own ./GUIDE.md:387:types as well. For example, perhaps you frequently search "web" files, which ./GUIDE.md:388:consist of JavaScript, HTML and CSS: ./GUIDE.md:391:$ rg --type-add 'web:*.html' --type-add 'web:*.css' --type-add 'web:*.js' -tweb title ./GUIDE.md:394:or, more succinctly, ./GUIDE.md:397:$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -tweb title ./GUIDE.md:400:The above command defines a new type, `web`, corresponding to the glob ./GUIDE.md:401:`*.{html,css,js}`. It then applies the new filter with `-tweb` and searches for ./GUIDE.md:402:the pattern `title`. If you ran ./GUIDE.md:405:$ rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' --type-list ./GUIDE.md:408:Then you would see your `web` type show up in the list, even though it is not ./GUIDE.md:409:part of ripgrep's built-in types. ./GUIDE.md:411:It is important to stress here that the `--type-add` flag only applies to the ./GUIDE.md:412:current command. It does not add a new file type and save it somewhere in a ./GUIDE.md:413:persistent form. If you want a type to be available in every ripgrep command, ./GUIDE.md:414:then you should either create a shell alias: ./GUIDE.md:417:alias rg="rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}'" ./GUIDE.md:420:or add `--type-add=web:*.{html,css,js}` to your ripgrep configuration file. ./GUIDE.md:421:([Configuration files](#configuration-file) are covered in more detail later.) ./GUIDE.md:423:#### The special `all` file type ./GUIDE.md:425:A special option supported by the `--type` flag is `all`. `--type all` looks ./GUIDE.md:426:for a match in any of the supported file types listed by `--type-list`, ./GUIDE.md:427:including those added on the command line using `--type-add`. It's equivalent ./GUIDE.md:428:to the command `rg --type agda --type asciidoc --type asm ...`, where `...` ./GUIDE.md:429:stands for a list of `--type` flags for the rest of the types in `--type-list`. ./GUIDE.md:431:As an example, let's suppose you have a shell script in your current directory, ./GUIDE.md:432:`my-shell-script`, which includes a shell library, `my-shell-library.bash`. ./GUIDE.md:433:Both `rg --type sh` and `rg --type all` would only search for matches in ./GUIDE.md:434:`my-shell-library.bash`, not `my-shell-script`, because the globs matched ./GUIDE.md:435:by the `sh` file type don't include files without an extension. On the ./GUIDE.md:436:other hand, `rg --type-not all` would search `my-shell-script` but not ./GUIDE.md:437:`my-shell-library.bash`. ./GUIDE.md:439:### Replacements ./GUIDE.md:441:ripgrep provides a limited ability to modify its output by replacing matched ./GUIDE.md:442:text with some other text. This is easiest to explain with an example. Remember ./GUIDE.md:443:when we searched for the word `fast` in ripgrep's README? ./GUIDE.md:446:$ rg fast README.md ./GUIDE.md:447:75: faster than both. (N.B. It is not, strictly speaking, a "drop-in" replacement ./GUIDE.md:448:88: color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast while ./GUIDE.md:449:119:### Is it really faster than everything else? ./GUIDE.md:450:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast because: ./GUIDE.md:451:129: optimizations to make searching very fast. ./GUIDE.md:454:What if we wanted to *replace* all occurrences of `fast` with `FAST`? That's ./GUIDE.md:455:easy with ripgrep's `--replace` flag: ./GUIDE.md:458:$ rg fast README.md --replace FAST ./GUIDE.md:459:75: FASTer than both. (N.B. It is not, strictly speaking, a "drop-in" replacement ./GUIDE.md:460:88: color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays FAST while ./GUIDE.md:461:119:### Is it really FASTer than everything else? ./GUIDE.md:462:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is FAST because: ./GUIDE.md:463:129: optimizations to make searching very FAST. ./GUIDE.md:466:or, more succinctly, ./GUIDE.md:469:$ rg fast README.md -r FAST ./GUIDE.md:470:[snip] ./GUIDE.md:473:In essence, the `--replace` flag applies *only* to the matching portion of text ./GUIDE.md:474:in the output. If you instead wanted to replace an entire line of text, then ./GUIDE.md:475:you need to include the entire line in your match. For example: ./GUIDE.md:478:$ rg '^.*fast.*$' README.md -r FAST ./GUIDE.md:479:75:FAST ./GUIDE.md:480:88:FAST ./GUIDE.md:481:119:FAST ./GUIDE.md:482:124:FAST ./GUIDE.md:483:129:FAST ./GUIDE.md:486:Alternatively, you can combine the `--only-matching` (or `-o` for short) with ./GUIDE.md:487:the `--replace` flag to achieve the same result: ./GUIDE.md:490:$ rg fast README.md --only-matching --replace FAST ./GUIDE.md:491:75:FAST ./GUIDE.md:492:88:FAST ./GUIDE.md:493:119:FAST ./GUIDE.md:494:124:FAST ./GUIDE.md:495:129:FAST ./GUIDE.md:498:or, more succinctly, ./GUIDE.md:501:$ rg fast README.md -or FAST ./GUIDE.md:502:[snip] ./GUIDE.md:505:Finally, replacements can include capturing groups. For example, let's say ./GUIDE.md:506:we wanted to find all occurrences of `fast` followed by another word and ./GUIDE.md:507:join them together with a dash. The pattern we might use for that is ./GUIDE.md:508:`fast\s+(\w+)`, which matches `fast`, followed by any amount of whitespace, ./GUIDE.md:509:followed by any number of "word" characters. We put the `\w+` in a "capturing ./GUIDE.md:510:group" (indicated by parentheses) so that we can reference it later in our ./GUIDE.md:511:replacement string. For example: ./GUIDE.md:514:$ rg 'fast\s+(\w+)' README.md -r 'fast-$1' ./GUIDE.md:515:88: color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast-while ./GUIDE.md:516:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast-because: ./GUIDE.md:519:Our replacement string here, `fast-$1`, consists of `fast-` followed by the ./GUIDE.md:520:contents of the capturing group at index `1`. (Capturing groups actually start ./GUIDE.md:521:at index 0, but the `0`th capturing group always corresponds to the entire ./GUIDE.md:522:match. The capturing group at index `1` always corresponds to the first ./GUIDE.md:523:explicit capturing group found in the regex pattern.) ./GUIDE.md:525:Capturing groups can also be named, which is sometimes more convenient than ./GUIDE.md:526:using the indices. For example, the following command is equivalent to the ./GUIDE.md:527:above command: ./GUIDE.md:530:$ rg 'fast\s+(?P\w+)' README.md -r 'fast-$word' ./GUIDE.md:531:88: color and full Unicode support. Unlike GNU grep, `ripgrep` stays fast-while ./GUIDE.md:532:124:Summarizing, `ripgrep` is fast-because: ./GUIDE.md:535:It is important to note that ripgrep **will never modify your files**. The ./GUIDE.md:536:`--replace` flag only controls ripgrep's output. (And there is no flag to let ./GUIDE.md:537:you do a replacement in a file.) ./GUIDE.md:540:### Configuration file ./GUIDE.md:542:It is possible that ripgrep's default options aren't suitable in every case. ./GUIDE.md:543:For that reason, and because shell aliases aren't always convenient, ripgrep ./GUIDE.md:544:supports configuration files. ./GUIDE.md:546:Setting up a configuration file is simple. ripgrep will not look in any ./GUIDE.md:547:predetermined directory for a config file automatically. Instead, you need to ./GUIDE.md:548:set the `RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH` environment variable to the file path of your ./GUIDE.md:549:config file. Once the environment variable is set, open the file and just type ./GUIDE.md:550:in the flags you want set automatically. There are only two rules for ./GUIDE.md:551:describing the format of the config file: ./GUIDE.md:553:1. Every line is a shell argument, after trimming whitespace. ./GUIDE.md:554:2. Lines starting with `#` (optionally preceded by any amount of whitespace) ./GUIDE.md:555:are ignored. ./GUIDE.md:557:In particular, there is no escaping. Each line is given to ripgrep as a single ./GUIDE.md:558:command line argument verbatim. ./GUIDE.md:560:Here's an example of a configuration file, which demonstrates some of the ./GUIDE.md:561:formatting peculiarities: ./GUIDE.md:564:$ cat $HOME/.ripgreprc ./GUIDE.md:565:# Don't let ripgrep vomit really long lines to my terminal, and show a preview. ./GUIDE.md:566:--max-columns=150 ./GUIDE.md:567:--max-columns-preview ./GUIDE.md:569:# Add my 'web' type. ./GUIDE.md:570:--type-add ./GUIDE.md:571:web:*.{html,css,js}* ./GUIDE.md:573:# Search hidden files / directories (e.g. dotfiles) by default ./GUIDE.md:574:--hidden ./GUIDE.md:576:# Using glob patterns to include/exclude files or folders ./GUIDE.md:577:--glob=!.git/* ./GUIDE.md:579:# or ./GUIDE.md:580:--glob ./GUIDE.md:581:!.git/* ./GUIDE.md:583:# Set the colors. ./GUIDE.md:584:--colors=line:none ./GUIDE.md:585:--colors=line:style:bold ./GUIDE.md:587:# Because who cares about case!? ./GUIDE.md:588:--smart-case ./GUIDE.md:591:When we use a flag that has a value, we either put the flag and the value on ./GUIDE.md:592:the same line but delimited by an `=` sign (e.g., `--max-columns=150`), or we ./GUIDE.md:593:put the flag and the value on two different lines. This is because ripgrep's ./GUIDE.md:594:argument parser knows to treat the single argument `--max-columns=150` as a ./GUIDE.md:595:flag with a value, but if we had written `--max-columns 150` in our ./GUIDE.md:596:configuration file, then ripgrep's argument parser wouldn't know what to do ./GUIDE.md:597:with it. ./GUIDE.md:599:Putting the flag and value on different lines is exactly equivalent and is a ./GUIDE.md:600:matter of style. ./GUIDE.md:602:Comments are encouraged so that you remember what the config is doing. Empty ./GUIDE.md:603:lines are OK too. ./GUIDE.md:605:So let's say you're using the above configuration file, but while you're at a ./GUIDE.md:606:terminal, you really want to be able to see lines longer than 150 columns. What ./GUIDE.md:607:do you do? Thankfully, all you need to do is pass `--max-columns 0` (or `-M0` ./GUIDE.md:608:for short) on the command line, which will override your configuration file's ./GUIDE.md:609:setting. This works because ripgrep's configuration file is *prepended* to the ./GUIDE.md:610:explicit arguments you give it on the command line. Since flags given later ./GUIDE.md:611:override flags given earlier, everything works as expected. This works for most ./GUIDE.md:612:other flags as well, and each flag's documentation states which other flags ./GUIDE.md:613:override it. ./GUIDE.md:615:If you're confused about what configuration file ripgrep is reading arguments ./GUIDE.md:616:from, then running ripgrep with the `--debug` flag should help clarify things. ./GUIDE.md:617:The debug output should note what config file is being loaded and the arguments ./GUIDE.md:618:that have been read from the configuration. ./GUIDE.md:620:Finally, if you want to make absolutely sure that ripgrep *isn't* reading a ./GUIDE.md:621:configuration file, then you can pass the `--no-config` flag, which will always ./GUIDE.md:622:prevent ripgrep from reading extraneous configuration from the environment, ./GUIDE.md:623:regardless of what other methods of configuration are added to ripgrep in the ./GUIDE.md:624:future. ./GUIDE.md:627:### File encoding ./GUIDE.md:629:[Text encoding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_encoding) is a complex ./GUIDE.md:630:topic, but we can try to summarize its relevancy to ripgrep: ./GUIDE.md:632:* Files are generally just a bundle of bytes. There is no reliable way to know ./GUIDE.md:633: their encoding. ./GUIDE.md:634:* Either the encoding of the pattern must match the encoding of the files being ./GUIDE.md:635: searched, or a form of transcoding must be performed that converts either the ./GUIDE.md:636: pattern or the file to the same encoding as the other. ./GUIDE.md:637:* ripgrep tends to work best on plain text files, and among plain text files, ./GUIDE.md:638: the most popular encodings likely consist of ASCII, latin1 or UTF-8. As ./GUIDE.md:639: a special exception, UTF-16 is prevalent in Windows environments ./GUIDE.md:641:In light of the above, here is how ripgrep behaves when `--encoding auto` is ./GUIDE.md:642:given, which is the default: ./GUIDE.md:644:* All input is assumed to be ASCII compatible (which means every byte that ./GUIDE.md:645: corresponds to an ASCII codepoint actually is an ASCII codepoint). This ./GUIDE.md:646: includes ASCII itself, latin1 and UTF-8. ./GUIDE.md:647:* ripgrep works best with UTF-8. For example, ripgrep's regular expression ./GUIDE.md:648: engine supports Unicode features. Namely, character classes like `\w` will ./GUIDE.md:649: match all word characters by Unicode's definition and `.` will match any ./GUIDE.md:650: Unicode codepoint instead of any byte. These constructions assume UTF-8, ./GUIDE.md:651: so they simply won't match when they come across bytes in a file that aren't ./GUIDE.md:652: UTF-8. ./GUIDE.md:653:* To handle the UTF-16 case, ripgrep will do something called "BOM sniffing" ./GUIDE.md:654: by default. That is, the first three bytes of a file will be read, and if ./GUIDE.md:655: they correspond to a UTF-16 BOM, then ripgrep will transcode the contents of ./GUIDE.md:656: the file from UTF-16 to UTF-8, and then execute the search on the transcoded ./GUIDE.md:657: version of the file. (This incurs a performance penalty since transcoding ./GUIDE.md:658: is needed in addition to regex searching.) If the file contains invalid ./GUIDE.md:659: UTF-16, then the Unicode replacement codepoint is substituted in place of ./GUIDE.md:660: invalid code units. ./GUIDE.md:661:* To handle other cases, ripgrep provides a `-E/--encoding` flag, which permits ./GUIDE.md:662: you to specify an encoding from the ./GUIDE.md:663: [Encoding Standard](https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#concept-encoding-get). ./GUIDE.md:664: ripgrep will assume *all* files searched are the encoding specified (unless ./GUIDE.md:665: the file has a BOM) and will perform a transcoding step just like in the ./GUIDE.md:666: UTF-16 case described above. ./GUIDE.md:668:By default, ripgrep will not require its input be valid UTF-8. That is, ripgrep ./GUIDE.md:669:can and will search arbitrary bytes. The key here is that if you're searching ./GUIDE.md:670:content that isn't UTF-8, then the usefulness of your pattern will degrade. If ./GUIDE.md:671:you're searching bytes that aren't ASCII compatible, then it's likely the ./GUIDE.md:672:pattern won't find anything. With all that said, this mode of operation is ./GUIDE.md:673:important, because it lets you find ASCII or UTF-8 *within* files that are ./GUIDE.md:674:otherwise arbitrary bytes. ./GUIDE.md:676:As a special case, the `-E/--encoding` flag supports the value `none`, which ./GUIDE.md:677:will completely disable all encoding related logic, including BOM sniffing. ./GUIDE.md:678:When `-E/--encoding` is set to `none`, ripgrep will search the raw bytes of ./GUIDE.md:679:the underlying file with no transcoding step. For example, here's how you might ./GUIDE.md:680:search the raw UTF-16 encoding of the string `Шерлок`: ./GUIDE.md:683:$ rg '(?-u)\(\x045\x04@\x04;\x04>\x04:\x04' -E none -a some-utf16-file ./GUIDE.md:686:Of course, that's just an example meant to show how one can drop down into ./GUIDE.md:687:raw bytes. Namely, the simpler command works as you might expect automatically: ./GUIDE.md:690:$ rg 'Шерлок' some-utf16-file ./GUIDE.md:693:Finally, it is possible to disable ripgrep's Unicode support from within the ./GUIDE.md:694:regular expression. For example, let's say you wanted `.` to match any byte ./GUIDE.md:695:rather than any Unicode codepoint. (You might want this while searching a ./GUIDE.md:696:binary file, since `.` by default will not match invalid UTF-8.) You could do ./GUIDE.md:697:this by disabling Unicode via a regular expression flag: ./GUIDE.md:700:$ rg '(?-u:.)' ./GUIDE.md:703:This works for any part of the pattern. For example, the following will find ./GUIDE.md:704:any Unicode word character followed by any ASCII word character followed by ./GUIDE.md:705:another Unicode word character: ./GUIDE.md:708:$ rg '\w(?-u:\w)\w' ./GUIDE.md:712:### Binary data ./GUIDE.md:714:In addition to skipping hidden files and files in your `.gitignore` by default, ./GUIDE.md:715:ripgrep also attempts to skip binary files. ripgrep does this by default ./GUIDE.md:716:because binary files (like PDFs or images) are typically not things you want to ./GUIDE.md:717:search when searching for regex matches. Moreover, if content in a binary file ./GUIDE.md:718:did match, then it's possible for undesirable binary data to be printed to your ./GUIDE.md:719:terminal and wreak havoc. ./GUIDE.md:721:Unfortunately, unlike skipping hidden files and respecting your `.gitignore` ./GUIDE.md:722:rules, a file cannot as easily be classified as binary. In order to figure out ./GUIDE.md:723:whether a file is binary, the most effective heuristic that balances ./GUIDE.md:724:correctness with performance is to simply look for `NUL` bytes. At that point, ./GUIDE.md:725:the determination is simple: a file is considered "binary" if and only if it ./GUIDE.md:726:contains a `NUL` byte somewhere in its contents. ./GUIDE.md:728:The issue is that while most binary files will have a `NUL` byte toward the ./GUIDE.md:729:beginning of its contents, this is not necessarily true. The `NUL` byte might ./GUIDE.md:730:be the very last byte in a large file, but that file is still considered ./GUIDE.md:731:binary. While this leads to a fair amount of complexity inside ripgrep's ./GUIDE.md:732:implementation, it also results in some unintuitive user experiences. ./GUIDE.md:734:At a high level, ripgrep operates in three different modes with respect to ./GUIDE.md:735:binary files: ./GUIDE.md:737:1. The default mode is to attempt to remove binary files from a search ./GUIDE.md:738: completely. This is meant to mirror how ripgrep removes hidden files and ./GUIDE.md:739: files in your `.gitignore` automatically. That is, as soon as a file is ./GUIDE.md:740: detected as binary, searching stops. If a match was already printed (because ./GUIDE.md:741: it was detected long before a `NUL` byte), then ripgrep will print a warning ./GUIDE.md:742: message indicating that the search stopped prematurely. This default mode ./GUIDE.md:743: **only applies to files searched by ripgrep as a result of recursive ./GUIDE.md:744: directory traversal**, which is consistent with ripgrep's other automatic ./GUIDE.md:745: filtering. For example, `rg foo .file` will search `.file` even though it ./GUIDE.md:746: is hidden. Similarly, `rg foo binary-file` will search `binary-file` in ./GUIDE.md:747: "binary" mode automatically. ./GUIDE.md:748:2. Binary mode is similar to the default mode, except it will not always ./GUIDE.md:749: stop searching after it sees a `NUL` byte. Namely, in this mode, ripgrep ./GUIDE.md:750: will continue searching a file that is known to be binary until the first ./GUIDE.md:751: of two conditions is met: 1) the end of the file has been reached or 2) a ./GUIDE.md:752: match is or has been seen. This means that in binary mode, if ripgrep ./GUIDE.md:753: reports no matches, then there are no matches in the file. When a match does ./GUIDE.md:754: occur, ripgrep prints a message similar to one it prints when in its default ./GUIDE.md:755: mode indicating that the search has stopped prematurely. This mode can be ./GUIDE.md:756: forcefully enabled for all files with the `--binary` flag. The purpose of ./GUIDE.md:757: binary mode is to provide a way to discover matches in all files, but to ./GUIDE.md:758: avoid having binary data dumped into your terminal. ./GUIDE.md:759:3. Text mode completely disables all binary detection and searches all files ./GUIDE.md:760: as if they were text. This is useful when searching a file that is ./GUIDE.md:761: predominantly text but contains a `NUL` byte, or if you are specifically ./GUIDE.md:762: trying to search binary data. This mode can be enabled with the `-a/--text` ./GUIDE.md:763: flag. Note that when using this mode on very large binary files, it is ./GUIDE.md:764: possible for ripgrep to use a lot of memory. ./GUIDE.md:766:Unfortunately, there is one additional complexity in ripgrep that can make it ./GUIDE.md:767:difficult to reason about binary files. That is, the way binary detection works ./GUIDE.md:768:depends on the way that ripgrep searches your files. Specifically: ./GUIDE.md:770:* When ripgrep uses memory maps, then binary detection is only performed on the ./GUIDE.md:771: first few kilobytes of the file in addition to every matching line. ./GUIDE.md:772:* When ripgrep doesn't use memory maps, then binary detection is performed on ./GUIDE.md:773: all bytes searched. ./GUIDE.md:775:This means that whether a file is detected as binary or not can change based ./GUIDE.md:776:on the internal search strategy used by ripgrep. If you prefer to keep ./GUIDE.md:777:ripgrep's binary file detection consistent, then you can disable memory maps ./GUIDE.md:778:via the `--no-mmap` flag. (The cost will be a small performance regression when ./GUIDE.md:779:searching very large files on some platforms.) ./GUIDE.md:782:### Preprocessor ./GUIDE.md:784:In ripgrep, a preprocessor is any type of command that can be run to transform ./GUIDE.md:785:the input of every file before ripgrep searches it. This makes it possible to ./GUIDE.md:786:search virtually any kind of content that can be automatically converted to ./GUIDE.md:787:text without having to teach ripgrep how to read said content. ./GUIDE.md:789:One common example is searching PDFs. PDFs are first and foremost meant to be ./GUIDE.md:790:displayed to users. But PDFs often have text streams in them that can be useful ./GUIDE.md:791:to search. In our case, we want to search Bruce Watson's excellent ./GUIDE.md:792:dissertation, ./GUIDE.md:793:[Taxonomies and Toolkits of Regular Language Algorithms](https://burntsushi.net/stuff/1995-watson.pdf). ./GUIDE.md:794:After downloading it, let's try searching it: ./GUIDE.md:797:$ rg 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.pdf ./GUIDE.md:801:Surely, a dissertation on regular language algorithms would mention ./GUIDE.md:802:Commentz-Walter. Indeed it does, but our search isn't picking it up because ./GUIDE.md:803:PDFs are a binary format, and the text shown in the PDF may not be encoded as ./GUIDE.md:804:simple contiguous UTF-8. Namely, even passing the `-a/--text` flag to ripgrep ./GUIDE.md:805:will not make our search work. ./GUIDE.md:807:One way to fix this is to convert the PDF to plain text first. This won't work ./GUIDE.md:808:well for all PDFs, but does great in a lot of cases. (Note that the tool we ./GUIDE.md:809:use, `pdftotext`, is part of the [poppler](https://poppler.freedesktop.org) ./GUIDE.md:810:PDF rendering library.) ./GUIDE.md:813:$ pdftotext 1995-watson.pdf > 1995-watson.txt ./GUIDE.md:814:$ rg 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.txt ./GUIDE.md:815:316:The Commentz-Walter algorithms : : : : : : : : : : : : : : : ./GUIDE.md:816:7165:4.4 The Commentz-Walter algorithms ./GUIDE.md:817:10062:in input string S , we obtain the Boyer-Moore algorithm. The Commentz-Walter algorithm ./GUIDE.md:818:17218:The Commentz-Walter algorithm (and its variants) displayed more interesting behaviour, ./GUIDE.md:819:17249:Aho-Corasick algorithms are used extensively. The Commentz-Walter algorithms are used ./GUIDE.md:820:17297: The Commentz-Walter algorithms (CW). In all versions of the CW algorithms, a common program skeleton is used with di erent shift functions. The CW algorithms are ./GUIDE.md:823:But having to explicitly convert every file can be a pain, especially when you ./GUIDE.md:824:have a directory full of PDF files. Instead, we can use ripgrep's preprocessor ./GUIDE.md:825:feature to search the PDF. ripgrep's `--pre` flag works by taking a single ./GUIDE.md:826:command name and then executing that command for every file that it searches. ./GUIDE.md:827:ripgrep passes the file path as the first and only argument to the command and ./GUIDE.md:828:also sends the contents of the file to stdin. So let's write a simple shell ./GUIDE.md:829:script that wraps `pdftotext` in a way that conforms to this interface: ./GUIDE.md:832:$ cat preprocess ./GUIDE.md:833:#!/bin/sh ./GUIDE.md:835:exec pdftotext - - ./GUIDE.md:838:With `preprocess` in the same directory as `1995-watson.pdf`, we can now use it ./GUIDE.md:839:to search the PDF: ./GUIDE.md:842:$ rg --pre ./preprocess 'The Commentz-Walter algorithm' 1995-watson.pdf ./GUIDE.md:843:316:The Commentz-Walter algorithms : : : : : : : : : : : : : : : ./GUIDE.md:844:7165:4.4 The Commentz-Walter algorithms ./GUIDE.md:845:10062:in input string S , we obtain the Boyer-Moore algorithm. The Commentz-Walter algorithm ./GUIDE.md:846:17218:The Commentz-Walter algorithm (and its variants) displayed more interesting behaviour, ./GUIDE.md:847:17249:Aho-Corasick algorithms are used extensively. This section ./GUIDE.md:991:is intended to give you a sampling of some of the most important and frequently ./GUIDE.md:992:used options that will likely impact how you use ripgrep on a regular basis. ./GUIDE.md:994:* `-h`: Show ripgrep's condensed help output. ./GUIDE.md:995:* `--help`: Show ripgrep's longer form help output. Usually this flag is put into ./GUIDE.md:1001: alias or a config file. ./GUIDE.md:1002:* `-F/--fixed-strings`: Disable regular expression matching and treat the pattern ./GUIDE.md:1003: as a literal string. ./GUIDE.md:1004:* `-w/--word-regexp`: Require that all matches of the pattern be surrounded ./GUIDE.md:1005: by word boundaries. That is, given `pattern`, the `--word-regexp` flag will ./GUIDE.md:1006: cause ripgrep to behave as if `pattern` were actually ./GUIDE.md:1007: `\b{start-half}(?:pattern)\b{end-half}`. ./GUIDE.md:1008: (Unlike `\b`, these half-boundaries don't require a word character on one ./GUIDE.md:1009: side. For example, `rg -w -e -2` will match `-2` in `(-2)` but `rg '\b-2\b'` ./GUIDE.md:1010: will not.) ./GUIDE.md:1011:* `-c/--count`: Report a count of total matched lines. ./GUIDE.md:1012:* `--files`: Print the files that ripgrep *would* search, but don't actually ./GUIDE.md:1013: search them. ./GUIDE.md:1014:* `-a/--text`: Search binary files as if they were plain text. ./GUIDE.md:1015:* `-U/--multiline`: Permit matches to span multiple lines. ./GUIDE.md:1016:* `-z/--search-zip`: Search compressed files (gzip, bzip2, lzma, xz, lz4, ./GUIDE.md:1017: brotli, zstd). This is disabled by default. ./GUIDE.md:1018:* `-C/--context`: Show the lines surrounding a match. ./GUIDE.md:1019:* `--sort path`: Force ripgrep to sort its output by file name. (This disables ./GUIDE.md:1020: parallelism, so it might be slower.) ./GUIDE.md:1021:* `-L/--follow`: Follow symbolic links while recursively searching. ./GUIDE.md:1022:* `-M/--max-columns`: Limit the length of lines printed by ripgrep. ./GUIDE.md:1023:* `--debug`: Shows ripgrep's debug output.
